title: Subject Matter
summary: Defines the purpose of the AI Act: improve the internal market, promote human-centric trustworthy AI, and ensure a high level of protection for health, safety, fundamental rights, democracy, rule of law, and environmental protection.
body: Art. 1(1) states the purpose of this Regulation: to improve the functioning of the internal market and promote the uptake of human-centric and trustworthy artificial intelligence (AI), while ensuring a high level of protection of health, safety, and fundamental rights enshrined in the Charter, including democracy, rule of law, and environmental protection, against harmful effects of AI systems in the Union, and to support innovation. Art. 1(2) lays down: (a) harmonised rules for the placing on the market, putting into service, and use of AI systems in the Union; (b) prohibitions of certain AI practices; (c) specific requirements for high-risk AI systems and obligations for operators of such systems; (d) harmonised transparency rules for certain AI systems; (e) harmonised rules for the placing on the market of general-purpose AI models; (f) rules on market monitoring, governance, and market surveillance enforcement; (g) measures to support innovation with particular focus on SMEs, including start-ups.
enforcementConsequence: No direct fine provision — violations may be sanctionable via Art. 16/26 umbrella obligations

title: Scope
summary: Defines who is subject to the AI Act (providers, deployers, importers, distributors, product manufacturers, authorised representatives, affected persons) and lists exemptions (military/national security, research, personal use, open source under conditions).
body: Art. 2(1) defines the personal scope: the Regulation applies to (a) providers placing on the market or putting into service AI systems or placing on the market general-purpose AI models in the Union, regardless of establishment; (b) deployers of AI systems with their seat in or located in the Union; (c) providers and deployers in third countries where the AI system output is used in the Union; (d) importers and distributors of AI systems; (e) product manufacturers placing AI systems on the market under their own name or trademark; (f) authorised representatives of providers not established in the Union; (g) affected persons located in the Union. Art. 2(2) provides that for high-risk AI systems classified under Art. 6(1) related to products covered by Annex I Section B harmonisation legislation, only Art. 6(1), Art. 102-109, and Art. 112 apply; Art. 57 applies only insofar as the high-risk AI requirements have been integrated into those harmonisation acts. Art. 2(3) limits the Regulation to areas falling under Union law and excludes AI systems used exclusively for military, defence, or national security purposes, regardless of the type of entity. Art. 2(4) excludes third-country public authorities and international organisations using AI in the context of international law enforcement or judicial cooperation agreements, provided adequate fundamental rights safeguards are in place. Art. 2(5) preserves intermediary service provider liability rules under Regulation 2022/2065. Art. 2(6) excludes AI systems or models developed and put into service solely for scientific research and development. Art. 2(7) preserves Union data protection law (GDPR, Regulation 2018/1725, Directives 2002/58/EC and 2016/680), without prejudice to Art. 10(5) and Art. 59. Art. 2(8) excludes research, testing, and development activities on AI systems before placing on the market or putting into service; real-world testing is not excluded. Art. 2(9) preserves other Union consumer protection and product safety legislation. Art. 2(10) excludes natural persons using AI systems for purely personal, non-professional activities. Art. 2(11) preserves Member State and Union authority to maintain or introduce more favourable worker protection rules. Art. 2(12) excludes AI systems released under free and open-source licences, unless they are high-risk AI systems or fall under Art. 5 or Art. 50.
enforcementConsequence: No direct fine provision — violations may be sanctionable via Art. 16/26 umbrella obligations

title: Definitions
summary: Provides 68 definitions for the AI Act including AI system, risk, provider, deployer, high-risk AI system, general-purpose AI model, serious incident, biometric identification, AI literacy, and deep fake.
body: Art. 3 defines 68 terms for the purposes of the Regulation. Key definitions include: (1) 'AI system' — a machine-based system designed to operate with varying levels of autonomy and that may exhibit adaptiveness after deployment, and that derives from received inputs how to generate outputs such as predictions, content, recommendations or decisions that can influence physical or virtual environments; (2) 'risk' — the combination of the probability of occurrence of harm and the severity of that harm; (3) 'provider' — a natural or legal person, public authority, agency or other body that develops or has developed an AI system or general-purpose AI model and places it on the market or puts it into service under its own name or trademark; (4) 'deployer' — a natural or legal person, public authority, agency or other body using an AI system under its authority, except where used for personal non-professional activity; (5) 'authorised representative' — a natural or legal person in the Union written-authorised by a provider; (6) 'importer'; (7) 'distributor'; (8) 'operator' — a provider, product manufacturer, deployer, authorised representative, importer or distributor; (9) 'placing on the market'; (10) 'making available on the market'; (11) 'putting into service'; (12) 'intended purpose'; (13) 'reasonably foreseeable misuse'; (14) 'safety component'; (15) 'instructions for use'; (16-18) 'recall', 'withdrawal', 'performance' of an AI system; (19-22) 'notifying authority', 'conformity assessment', 'conformity assessment body', 'notified body'; (23) 'substantial modification'; (24) 'CE marking'; (25) 'post-market monitoring system'; (26) 'market surveillance authority'; (27) 'harmonised standard'; (28) 'common specification'; (29-33) 'training data', 'validation data', 'validation data set', 'testing data', 'input data'; (34-36) 'biometric data', 'biometric identification', 'biometric verification'; (37) 'special categories of personal data'; (38) 'sensitive operational data'; (39) 'emotion recognition system'; (40) 'biometric categorisation system'; (41-43) 'remote biometric identification system', 'real-time remote biometric identification system', 'post remote biometric identification system'; (44) 'publicly accessible space'; (45-46) 'law enforcement authority', 'law enforcement'; (47) 'AI Office'; (48) 'national competent authority'; (49) 'serious incident' — an incident or malfunction directly or indirectly causing (a) death or serious health damage, (b) serious and irreversible disruption of critical infrastructure management, (c) breach of fundamental rights obligations, (d) serious property or environmental damage; (50-52) 'personal data', 'non-personal data', 'profiling'; (53-55) 'real-world testing plan', 'sandbox plan', 'AI regulatory sandbox'; (56) 'AI literacy' — the skills, knowledge, and understanding enabling providers, deployers, and affected persons to deploy AI systems in an informed manner and become aware of AI opportunities, risks, and potential harms; (57) 'real-world testing'; (58) 'testing subject'; (59) 'informed consent'; (60) 'deep fake' — AI-generated or manipulated image, audio or video content resembling real persons, objects, places, entities or events that would falsely appear authentic or truthful to a person; (61) 'widespread infringement'; (62) 'critical infrastructure'; (63) 'general-purpose AI model' — an AI model, including when trained with large amounts of data using self-supervision at scale, that displays significant generality and is capable of competently performing a wide range of distinct tasks regardless of how it is placed on the market, and can be integrated into a variety of downstream systems or applications; (64) 'high-impact capabilities'; (65) 'systemic risk'; (66) 'general-purpose AI system'; (67) 'floating point operation'; (68) 'downstream provider'.
enforcementConsequence: No direct fine provision — violations may be sanctionable via Art. 16/26 umbrella obligations

title: AI Literacy
summary: Requires providers and deployers to take measures to ensure sufficient AI literacy of their staff and other persons operating AI systems on their behalf, taking into account technical knowledge, experience, education, context of use, and affected persons.
body: Art. 4 requires providers and deployers of AI systems to take measures to ensure, to the best of their abilities, that their staff and other persons dealing with the operation and use of AI systems on their behalf have a sufficient level of AI literacy, taking into account their technical knowledge, experience, education and training, and the context in which the AI systems are to be used, as well as the persons or groups of persons on whom the AI systems are to be used.
enforcementConsequence: No direct fine provision — violations may be sanctionable via Art. 16 (provider) or Art. 26 (deployer) umbrella obligations

title: Prohibited AI Practices
summary: Prohibits eight categories of AI practices: subliminal manipulation, vulnerability exploitation, social scoring, individual predictive policing, untargeted facial image scraping, workplace/education emotion recognition, biometric categorisation by sensitive attributes, and real-time remote biometric identification in public spaces for law enforcement (with narrow exceptions requiring judicial authorisation).
body: Art. 5(1) prohibits the following AI practices: (a) placing on the market, putting into service, or use of an AI system that deploys subliminal techniques beyond a person's consciousness or purposefully manipulative or deceptive techniques, with the objective or effect of materially distorting a person's or group's behaviour by appreciably impairing their ability to make an informed decision, thereby causing them to take a decision they would not have otherwise taken, in a manner causing or likely to cause significant harm; (b) placing on the market, putting into service, or use of an AI system that exploits a vulnerability or special condition of a natural person or specific group due to age, disability, or a specific social or economic situation, with the objective or effect of materially distorting their behaviour in a manner causing or likely to cause significant harm; (c) placing on the market, putting into service, or use of AI systems for evaluating or classifying natural persons or groups over a certain period based on their social behaviour or known, inferred, or predicted personal characteristics, where the social scoring leads to: (i) detrimental or unfavourable treatment in social contexts unrelated to the circumstances in which the data was originally generated or collected; (ii) detrimental or unfavourable treatment that is unjustified or disproportionate to the social behaviour or its gravity; (d) placing on the market, putting into service, or use of an AI system for risk assessments of natural persons to assess or predict the risk of committing a criminal offence based solely on profiling or on assessment of personality traits and characteristics; this prohibition does not apply to AI systems supporting human-conducted assessments of involvement in criminal activity based on objective and verifiable facts directly linked to criminal activity; (e) placing on the market, putting into service, or use of AI systems that create or expand facial recognition databases through untargeted scraping of facial images from the internet or CCTV footage; (f) placing on the market, putting into service, or use of AI systems to infer emotions of natural persons in the workplace and in educational institutions, except where intended for medical or safety reasons; (g) placing on the market, putting into service, or use of biometric categorisation systems individually categorising natural persons based on biometric data to deduce or infer their race, political opinions, trade union membership, religious or philosophical beliefs, sex life, or sexual orientation; this prohibition does not apply to labelling or filtering of lawfully acquired biometric datasets or categorisation of biometric data in the area of law enforcement; (h) use of real-time remote biometric identification systems in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement purposes, except where and insofar as strictly necessary for: (i) targeted search for specific victims of abduction, trafficking, or sexual exploitation, and search for missing persons; (ii) prevention of a specific, substantial, and imminent threat to life or physical safety of natural persons or a genuine and present or foreseeable threat of a terrorist attack; (iii) locating or identifying a person suspected of having committed a criminal offence for the purpose of criminal investigation, prosecution, or execution of a criminal penalty for offences listed in Annex II punishable by a custodial sentence of at least four years. Art. 5(2) restricts the use of real-time remote biometric identification under paragraph 1(h) to identity confirmation of specifically targeted persons, considering (a) the nature of the situation and (b) consequences for the rights and freedoms of all persons affected. Additionally, necessary and proportionate safeguards must be observed per national law, including temporal, geographical, and personal limitations. Use is only permitted after the law enforcement authority has completed a fundamental rights impact assessment per Art. 27 and registered the system per Art. 49 in the EU database; in duly justified urgent cases, use may begin without registration provided registration follows without delay. Art. 5(3) requires prior authorisation from a judicial authority or independent administrative authority for each use of a real-time remote biometric identification system; in duly justified urgent cases, use may begin without authorisation provided it is sought within 24 hours. The authorising authority grants authorisation only if satisfied, based on objective evidence, that the use is necessary and proportionate and limited to what is strictly necessary in terms of time, geography, and personal scope. Decisions with adverse legal effects may not be taken solely on the basis of the system output. Art. 5(4) requires each use to be notified to the market surveillance authority and national data protection authority per national rules. Art. 5(5) permits Member States to provide for full or partial authorisation of real-time remote biometric identification within the limits of paragraph 1(h) and paragraphs 2-3; Member States must lay down detailed rules and notify the Commission within 30 days. Art. 5(6) requires national market surveillance and data protection authorities to submit annual reports to the Commission on such use. Art. 5(7) requires the Commission to publish annual reports based on aggregated Member State data, excluding sensitive operational data. Art. 5(8) clarifies that Art. 5 does not affect prohibitions that apply where AI practices violate other Union law.
enforcementConsequence: Fines up to EUR 35 000 000 or 7% of total worldwide annual turnover (Art. 99(3))

title: Classification Rules for High-Risk AI Systems
summary: Establishes two pathways for high-risk classification: (1) AI systems as safety components of products subject to third-party conformity assessment under Annex I harmonisation legislation, and (2) AI systems listed in Annex III. Provides exceptions where Annex III systems are not high-risk if they pose no significant risk, with conditions.
body: Art. 6(1) classifies an AI system as high-risk if two conditions are met: (a) the AI system is intended to be used as a safety component of a product falling under the Annex I Union harmonisation legislation, or the AI system is itself such a product; and (b) the product whose safety component is the AI system, or the AI system itself as a product, must undergo third-party conformity assessment for placing on the market or putting into service under the Annex I Union harmonisation legislation. Art. 6(2) additionally classifies AI systems referred to in Annex III as high-risk. Art. 6(3) provides an exception: an Annex III AI system is not considered high-risk if it does not pose a significant risk of harm to health, safety, or fundamental rights, including by not materially influencing decision-making outcomes. This exception applies if one of the following conditions is met: (a) the AI system is intended to perform a narrow procedural task; (b) the AI system is intended to improve the result of a previously completed human activity; (c) the AI system is intended to detect decision patterns or deviations from prior decision patterns and is not meant to replace or influence the previously completed human assessment without appropriate human review; or (d) the AI system is intended to perform a preparatory task for an assessment relevant to the Annex III use cases. Notwithstanding, an Annex III AI system is always considered high-risk when it performs profiling of natural persons. Art. 6(4) requires a provider who considers an Annex III AI system as not high-risk to document this assessment before placing on the market or putting into service; the provider is subject to registration under Art. 49(2) and must present the documentation upon request of national competent authorities. Art. 6(5) requires the Commission, after consulting the AI Board, to provide guidelines and a comprehensive list of practical examples of high-risk and non-high-risk use cases by 2 February 2026. Art. 6(6) empowers the Commission to adopt delegated acts per Art. 97 to amend the exception conditions in paragraph 3(2) by adding new conditions or modifying existing ones. Art. 6(7) empowers the Commission to adopt delegated acts to amend the exception conditions by deleting conditions where necessary to maintain the level of protection. Art. 6(8) requires that any amendment to the exception conditions must not lower the general level of protection and must ensure coherence with delegated acts under Art. 7(1).
enforcementConsequence: No direct fine provision — violations may be sanctionable via Art. 16 (provider) umbrella obligations

title: Amendments to Annex III
summary: Empowers the Commission to amend the Annex III high-risk AI use case list via delegated acts, adding, modifying, or removing use cases based on risk criteria including intended purpose, scale of use, data types, autonomy, severity of harm, power imbalance, and existing legal remedies.
body: Art. 7(1) empowers the Commission to adopt delegated acts per Art. 97 to amend Annex III by adding or modifying use cases for high-risk AI systems, where both conditions are met: (a) the AI systems are intended for deployment in one of the areas listed in Annex III; and (b) the AI systems pose a risk of harm to health and safety or have adverse effects on fundamental rights, and that risk equals or exceeds the risk posed by high-risk AI systems already listed in Annex III. Art. 7(2) lists the criteria the Commission must consider when assessing condition (b): (a) intended purpose; (b) extent of use or expected use; (c) nature and extent of data processed, particularly whether special categories of personal data are processed; (d) extent of AI system autonomy and possibility of human override of potentially harmful decisions; (e) extent to which AI system use has already caused harm to health, safety, or fundamental rights, or has given rise to significant concerns; (f) potential scale of harm, particularly its intensity and capacity to affect multiple persons or disproportionately affect specific groups; (g) extent to which affected persons depend on the AI system outcome, particularly where it is practically or legally unreasonable to avoid the outcome; (h) extent of power imbalance or vulnerability of affected persons vis-a-vis the AI system operator, particularly due to status, authority, knowledge, economic or social circumstances, or age; (i) extent to which the outcome is easily reversible or correctable, noting that outcomes negatively affecting health, safety, or fundamental rights are not considered easily reversible; (j) extent and likelihood that the AI system is beneficial for individuals, groups, or society, including possible product safety improvements; (k) extent to which existing Union law provides (i) effective remedies other than damages claims, (ii) effective measures to prevent or substantially reduce risks. Art. 7(3) empowers the Commission to adopt delegated acts to remove high-risk AI systems from Annex III where both conditions are met: (a) the system no longer poses significant risks to fundamental rights, health, or safety considering the paragraph 2 criteria; (b) deletion does not lower the general level of protection under Union law.
enforcementConsequence: No direct fine provision — Commission delegation mechanism

title: Compliance with Requirements
summary: Requires high-risk AI systems to comply with the requirements of Chapter III Section 2 (Art. 9-15), taking into account intended purpose and the generally acknowledged state of the art, with the risk management system under Art. 9 as the compliance framework. Allows integration with existing product harmonisation documentation.
body: Art. 8(1) requires high-risk AI systems to meet the requirements laid down in Chapter III Section 2, taking into account their intended purpose and the generally acknowledged state of the art in AI and AI-related technologies. The risk management system referred to in Art. 9 shall be taken into account when ensuring compliance with these requirements. Art. 8(2) provides that where a product contains an AI system subject to both this Regulation and the Annex I Section A Union harmonisation legislation, providers are responsible for ensuring full compliance with all applicable requirements. To ensure coherence, avoid duplication, and minimise additional burden, providers may integrate the required testing, reporting procedures, information, and documentation with existing documentation and procedures required under the Annex I Section A harmonisation legislation.
enforcementConsequence: No direct fine provision — violations sanctionable via Art. 16 (provider) umbrella obligations (Art. 99(4)(a): fines up to EUR 15 000 000 or 3%)

title: Risk Management System
summary: Requires a continuous, iterative risk management system for high-risk AI systems throughout their lifecycle, covering risk identification, assessment, mitigation, and testing. Residual risks must be judged acceptable. Special consideration for minors and vulnerable groups.
body: Art. 9(1) requires a risk management system to be established, applied, documented, and maintained for high-risk AI systems. Art. 9(2) defines the risk management system as a continuous iterative process planned and executed throughout the entire lifecycle, requiring regular systematic review and updating. It comprises the following steps: (a) identification and analysis of known and reasonably foreseeable risks that the high-risk AI system may pose to health, safety, or fundamental rights when used in accordance with its intended purpose; (b) estimation and evaluation of the risks that may arise when the system is used in accordance with its intended purpose or under conditions of reasonably foreseeable misuse; (c) evaluation of other risks that may materialise based on analysis of data from the post-market monitoring system referred to in Art. 72; (d) adoption of appropriate and targeted risk management measures to address the risks identified under (a). Art. 9(3) limits the scope to risks that can reasonably be mitigated or eliminated through the development or design of the high-risk AI system or through the provision of adequate technical information. Art. 9(4) requires risk management measures under paragraph 2(d) to give due consideration to the effects and possible interactions resulting from the combined application of the Section 2 requirements, to minimise risks more effectively while ensuring appropriate balance. Art. 9(5) requires risk management measures to be designed so that each relevant residual risk associated with each hazard, as well as the overall residual risk, is judged acceptable. In determining the most appropriate measures: (a) elimination or reduction of identified and assessed risks through appropriate design and development, as far as technically feasible; (b) where appropriate, adequate mitigation and control measures for risks that cannot be eliminated; (c) provision of information required by Art. 13 and, where appropriate, training of deployers. The technical knowledge, experience, education expected of the deployer and the presumable context of use must be duly considered. Art. 9(6) requires high-risk AI systems to be tested to identify the most appropriate targeted risk management measures, ensuring consistent performance in accordance with intended purpose and compliance with Section 2 requirements. Art. 9(7) permits testing procedures to include real-world testing per Art. 60. Art. 9(8) requires testing at any appropriate time during the development process and in any case before placing on the market or putting into service, using pre-defined metrics and probabilistic thresholds appropriate for the intended purpose. Art. 9(9) requires providers to consider whether, given its intended purpose, the high-risk AI system is likely to have adverse effects on persons under 18 or other vulnerable groups. Art. 9(10) allows providers subject to internal risk management requirements under other relevant Union law to integrate the aspects of paragraphs 1-9 into or combine them with those procedures.
enforcementConsequence: No direct fine provision — violations sanctionable via Art. 16 (provider) umbrella obligations (Art. 99(4)(a): fines up to EUR 15 000 000 or 3%)

title: Data and Data Governance
summary: Requires high-risk AI systems using data-trained models to be developed with training, validation, and test datasets meeting quality criteria. Mandates data governance procedures covering design decisions, collection, preparation, bias examination, and gap analysis. Permits processing of special categories of personal data for bias detection under strict conditions.
body: Art. 10(1) requires high-risk AI systems employing techniques involving training of AI models with data to be developed with training, validation, and test datasets that meet the quality criteria specified in paragraphs 2-5, where such datasets are used. Art. 10(2) mandates data governance and data management practices appropriate to the intended purpose of the high-risk AI system, covering in particular: (a) relevant design choices; (b) data collection processes and the origin of data, and in the case of personal data, the original purpose of data collection; (c) relevant data preparation operations such as annotation, labelling, cleaning, updating, enrichment, and aggregation; (d) the formulation of assumptions, in particular with respect to the information that the data are supposed to measure and represent; (e) an assessment of the availability, quantity, and suitability of the data sets needed; (f) examination in view of possible biases that are likely to affect health and safety, negatively impact fundamental rights, or lead to discrimination prohibited under Union law, in particular where data outputs influence inputs for future operations; (g) appropriate measures to detect, prevent, and mitigate possible biases identified under (f); (h) identification of relevant data gaps or shortcomings that prevent compliance with this Regulation, and how those gaps and shortcomings can be addressed. Art. 10(3) requires training, validation, and test datasets to be relevant, sufficiently representative, and to the best extent possible free from errors and complete, having regard to the intended purpose. They must have the appropriate statistical properties, including in relation to the persons or groups on whom the high-risk AI system is intended to be used. These properties may be met at the level of individual datasets or a combination thereof. Art. 10(4) requires datasets to take account of the characteristics or elements particular to the specific geographical, contextual, behavioural, or functional setting within which the high-risk AI system is intended to be used, to the extent required by the intended purpose. Art. 10(5) permits providers, to the extent strictly necessary for ensuring bias detection and correction in relation to high-risk AI systems in accordance with paragraph 2(f) and (g), to exceptionally process special categories of personal data, subject to appropriate safeguards for fundamental rights and freedoms. In addition to the provisions of Regulations 2016/679 and 2018/1725 and Directive 2016/680, all of the following conditions must be met: (a) bias detection and correction cannot be effectively carried out by processing other data, including synthetic or anonymised data; (b) the special categories of personal data are subject to technical limitations on re-use and state-of-the-art security and privacy-preserving measures, including pseudonymisation; (c) the data are subject to measures ensuring they are secured, protected, and subject to adequate safeguards, including strict access controls and documentation to prevent misuse; (d) the data are not transmitted or transferred to third parties; (e) the data are deleted once the bias has been corrected or the retention period has expired, whichever comes first; (f) the records of processing activities under the applicable data protection regulations include the reasons why the processing of special categories was strictly necessary and why it could not be achieved by processing other data. Art. 10(6) provides that for high-risk AI systems not employing techniques involving training of AI models, paragraphs 2-5 apply only to test datasets.
enforcementConsequence: No direct fine provision — violations sanctionable via Art. 16 (provider) umbrella obligations (Art. 99(4)(a): fines up to EUR 15 000 000 or 3%)

title: Technical Documentation
summary: Requires providers to prepare and maintain technical documentation for high-risk AI systems before placing on the market, demonstrating compliance with Section 2 requirements. Must contain at least the information specified in Annex IV. SMEs may use a simplified form.
body: Art. 11(1) requires the technical documentation of a high-risk AI system to be drawn up before that system is placed on the market or put into service, and to be kept up to date. The technical documentation must demonstrate how the high-risk AI system complies with the Section 2 requirements and provide national competent authorities and notified bodies with the information in a clear and comprehensible form necessary to assess compliance. It must contain at least the information referred to in Annex IV. SMEs, including start-ups, may provide the elements of the technical documentation in simplified form. The Commission shall draw up a simplified form tailored to the needs of small and micro enterprises. Notified bodies shall accept the form for conformity assessment purposes. Art. 11(2) provides that where a high-risk AI system related to a product covered by Annex I Section A Union harmonisation legislation is placed on the market or put into service, a single technical documentation shall be drawn up containing the information required by paragraph 1 and the information required by those legal acts. Art. 11(3) empowers the Commission to adopt delegated acts per Art. 97 to amend Annex IV where necessary to ensure that the technical documentation continues to contain all information necessary to assess compliance with the Section 2 requirements in light of technical progress.
enforcementConsequence: No direct fine provision — violations sanctionable via Art. 16 (provider) umbrella obligations (Art. 99(4)(a): fines up to EUR 15 000 000 or 3%)

title: Record-Keeping
summary: Requires high-risk AI systems to enable automatic logging of events throughout the system lifecycle. Logging must support traceability for risk identification, post-market monitoring, and deployer oversight. Biometric identification systems (Annex III No. 1(a)) have additional specific logging requirements.
body: Art. 12(1) requires the technology of high-risk AI systems to enable automatic recording of events (logging) over the lifetime of the system. Art. 12(2) requires logging capabilities to ensure traceability of the functioning of the high-risk AI system to a degree appropriate to its intended purpose, enabling the recording of events relevant for: (a) identifying situations that may result in the high-risk AI system presenting a risk within the meaning of Art. 79(1) or in a substantial modification; (b) facilitating post-market monitoring pursuant to Art. 72; and (c) monitoring the operation of high-risk AI systems pursuant to Art. 26(5). Art. 12(3) requires the logging capabilities of the high-risk AI systems referred to in Annex III point 1(a) to include at least: (a) recording of each period of use of the system (date and time of the start and end of each use); (b) the reference database against which the system checks input data; (c) the input data for which the query has led to a match; (d) the identity of the natural persons involved in the verification of the results pursuant to Art. 14(5).
enforcementConsequence: No direct fine provision — violations sanctionable via Art. 16 (provider) umbrella obligations (Art. 99(4)(a): fines up to EUR 15 000 000 or 3%)

title: Transparency and Provision of Information to Deployers
summary: Requires high-risk AI systems to be designed for sufficient operational transparency so deployers can interpret and use outputs appropriately. Systems must be accompanied by instructions for use containing detailed information on capabilities, limitations, accuracy, intended purpose, human oversight measures, and logging mechanisms.
body: Art. 13(1) requires high-risk AI systems to be designed and developed so that their operation is sufficiently transparent to enable deployers to interpret a system's output and use it appropriately. Transparency shall be ensured in an appropriate type and to an appropriate degree to enable providers and deployers to comply with their relevant obligations under Section 3. Art. 13(2) requires high-risk AI systems to be accompanied by instructions for use in an appropriate digital format or otherwise, containing concise, complete, correct, and clear information that is relevant, accessible, and comprehensible to deployers. Art. 13(3) requires the instructions for use to contain at least the following: (a) the name and contact details of the provider and, where applicable, its authorised representative; (b) the characteristics, capabilities, and limitations of performance of the high-risk AI system, including: (i) its intended purpose; (ii) the level of accuracy — including relevant metrics —, robustness, and cybersecurity per Art. 15 for which the system has been tested and validated and which can be expected, and any known and foreseeable circumstances that may affect that expected level; (iii) any known or foreseeable circumstances related to use in accordance with intended purpose or reasonably foreseeable misuse that may lead to risks to health, safety, or fundamental rights per Art. 9(2); (iv) where applicable, the technical capabilities and characteristics of the system to provide information relevant to explain its outputs; (v) where applicable, its performance regarding specific persons or groups of persons on which the system is intended to be used; (vi) where applicable, specifications for the input data or any other relevant information on the training, validation, and testing datasets used, having regard to the intended purpose; (vii) where applicable, information enabling deployers to interpret the output and use the system appropriately; (c) any changes to the high-risk AI system and its performance that have been pre-determined by the provider at the time of the initial conformity assessment; (d) the human oversight measures referred to in Art. 14, including the technical measures put in place to facilitate the interpretation of the outputs by deployers; (e) the computational and hardware resources required, the expected lifetime of the system, and any necessary maintenance and care measures including their frequency to ensure proper functioning, including as regards software updates; (f) where applicable, a description of the mechanisms included in the system that allow deployers to properly collect, store, and interpret the logs in accordance with Art. 12.
enforcementConsequence: No direct fine provision — violations sanctionable via Art. 16 (provider) umbrella obligations (Art. 99(4)(a): fines up to EUR 15 000 000 or 3%)

title: Human Oversight
summary: Requires high-risk AI systems to be designed for effective human oversight during use, including the ability to understand system capabilities and limitations, remain aware of automation bias, correctly interpret outputs, override or disregard outputs, and interrupt the system via a stop button. Biometric identification systems (Annex III No. 1(a)) require two-person verification.
body: Art. 14(1) requires high-risk AI systems to be designed and developed so that they can be effectively overseen by natural persons during the period of use, including through appropriate human-machine interface tools. Art. 14(2) states that human oversight serves to prevent or minimise risks to health, safety, or fundamental rights that may arise when a high-risk AI system is used in accordance with its intended purpose or under conditions of reasonably foreseeable misuse, in particular when such risks persist despite compliance with other Section 2 requirements. Art. 14(3) requires oversight measures to be commensurate with the risks, the degree of autonomy, and the context of use of the high-risk AI system, and to be ensured through one or both of: (a) measures identified by the provider and, where technically feasible, built into the system before placing on the market or putting into service; (b) measures identified by the provider and suitable for implementation by the deployer. Art. 14(4) requires the high-risk AI system to be provided to the deployer so that the natural persons assigned human oversight are appropriately and proportionately able to: (a) properly understand the relevant capabilities and limitations of the system and duly monitor its operation, including with regard to detecting and addressing anomalies, dysfunctions, and unexpected performance; (b) remain aware of the possible tendency of automatically relying on or over-relying on the output produced by a high-risk AI system (automation bias), in particular where systems output information or recommendations on which natural persons base decisions; (c) correctly interpret the output, taking into account the interpretation tools and methods available; (d) decide, in any particular situation, not to use the system or to disregard, override, or reverse the output; (e) intervene in the operation of the system or interrupt it through a stop button or similar procedure, allowing the system to come to a halt in a safe state. Art. 14(5) requires that for the high-risk AI systems referred to in Annex III point 1(a), the measures under paragraph 3 must additionally ensure that the deployer does not take any action or decision based solely on the identification produced by the system until that identification has been separately verified and confirmed by at least two natural persons with the necessary competence, training, and authority. The requirement for separate verification by at least two natural persons does not apply to high-risk AI systems used for law enforcement, migration, border control, or asylum purposes where applying this requirement would be disproportionate under Union or national law.
enforcementConsequence: No direct fine provision — violations sanctionable via Art. 16 (provider) umbrella obligations (Art. 99(4)(a): fines up to EUR 15 000 000 or 3%)

title: Accuracy, Robustness and Cybersecurity
summary: Requires high-risk AI systems to achieve appropriate levels of accuracy, robustness, and cybersecurity throughout their lifecycle. Robustness includes resilience against errors, feedback loops, and adversarial attacks. Cybersecurity measures must address AI-specific vulnerabilities including data poisoning, model poisoning, adversarial examples, and model evasion.
body: Art. 15(1) requires high-risk AI systems to be designed and developed to achieve an appropriate level of accuracy, robustness, and cybersecurity, and to perform consistently in those respects throughout their lifecycle. Art. 15(2) provides that the Commission, in cooperation with relevant stakeholders and organisations such as metrology and benchmarking authorities, shall where appropriate encourage the development of benchmarks and measurement methodologies for the technical aspects of measuring accuracy and robustness per paragraph 1 and other relevant performance metrics. Art. 15(3) requires the levels of accuracy and the relevant accuracy metrics of high-risk AI systems to be declared in the accompanying instructions for use. Art. 15(4) requires high-risk AI systems to be as resilient as possible against errors, faults, or inconsistencies that may occur within the system or the environment in which the system operates, in particular due to interaction with natural persons or other systems; technical and organisational measures shall be taken. Robustness may be achieved through technical redundancy, including backup or fail-safe plans. High-risk AI systems which continue to learn after being placed on the market or put into service shall be developed to eliminate or reduce as far as possible the risk of possibly biased outputs influencing input for future operations (feedback loops) and to ensure that appropriate mitigation measures are taken against such feedback loops. Art. 15(5) requires high-risk AI systems to be resilient against attempts by unauthorised third parties to alter their use, outputs, or performance by exploiting system vulnerabilities. Technical solutions for cybersecurity must be appropriate to the relevant circumstances and risks. Technical solutions to address AI-specific vulnerabilities shall include, where appropriate, measures to prevent, detect, respond to, resolve, and control attacks that attempt data poisoning or poisoning of pre-trained components used in training (model poisoning), inputs designed to cause the model to make errors (adversarial examples or model evasions), attacks on confidential data, or model flaws.
enforcementConsequence: No direct fine provision — violations sanctionable via Art. 16 (provider) umbrella obligations (Art. 99(4)(a): fines up to EUR 15 000 000 or 3%)

title: Obligations of Providers of High-Risk AI Systems
summary: Central umbrella provision listing all provider obligations for high-risk AI systems: ensure Section 2 compliance, labelling, quality management system (Art. 17), documentation retention (Art. 18), log retention (Art. 19), conformity assessment (Art. 43), EU declaration of conformity (Art. 47), CE marking (Art. 48), registration (Art. 49), corrective measures (Art. 20), cooperation with authorities (Art. 21), and accessibility.
body: Art. 16 requires providers of high-risk AI systems to: (a) ensure that their high-risk AI systems comply with the requirements laid down in Section 2; (b) indicate on the high-risk AI system or, where not possible, on its packaging or accompanying documentation, their name, registered trade name or registered trade mark, and the address at which they can be contacted; (c) have a quality management system in place which complies with Art. 17; (d) keep the documentation referred to in Art. 18; (e) keep the logs automatically generated by their high-risk AI systems as referred to in Art. 19, where under their control; (f) ensure that the high-risk AI system is subject to the relevant conformity assessment procedure referred to in Art. 43 before it is placed on the market or put into service; (g) draw up an EU declaration of conformity in accordance with Art. 47; (h) affix the CE marking to the high-risk AI system or, where not possible, on its packaging or accompanying documentation, to indicate conformity with this Regulation in accordance with Art. 48; (i) comply with the registration obligations referred to in Art. 49(1); (j) take the necessary corrective measures and provide the information required by Art. 20; (k) upon reasoned request by a national competent authority, demonstrate the conformity of the high-risk AI system with the requirements laid down in Section 2; (l) ensure that the high-risk AI system complies with accessibility requirements in accordance with Directives (EU) 2016/2102 and (EU) 2019/882.
enforcementConsequence: Fines up to EUR 15 000 000 or 3% of total worldwide annual turnover (Art. 99(4)(a))

title: Quality Management System
summary: Requires providers of high-risk AI systems to establish a documented quality management system covering regulatory compliance, design, development, testing, data management, risk management, post-market monitoring, incident reporting, communication with authorities, record-keeping, resource management, and accountability. Financial institutions may integrate QMS with existing internal governance requirements.
body: Art. 17(1) requires providers of high-risk AI systems to put in place a quality management system that ensures compliance with this Regulation. The system shall be systematically and orderly documented in the form of written policies, procedures, and instructions and shall comprise at least the following aspects: (a) a strategy for regulatory compliance, including compliance with conformity assessment procedures and procedures for the management of changes to the high-risk AI system; (b) techniques, procedures, and systematic actions for the design, design control, and design verification of the high-risk AI system; (c) techniques, procedures, and systematic actions for the development, quality control, and quality assurance of the high-risk AI system; (d) examination, test, and validation procedures to be carried out before, during, and after the development of the high-risk AI system, and the frequency of their performance; (e) technical specifications and standards to be applied, and where the relevant harmonised standards are not applied in full or do not cover all relevant Section 2 requirements, the means to be used to ensure compliance; (f) systems and procedures for data management, including data acquisition, data collection, data analysis, data labelling, data storage, data filtration, data mining, data aggregation, data retention, and any other operation regarding the data carried out before and for the purposes of placing on the market or putting into service; (g) the risk management system referred to in Art. 9; (h) the setting-up, implementation, and maintenance of a post-market monitoring system in accordance with Art. 72; (i) procedures related to the reporting of a serious incident in accordance with Art. 73; (j) the handling of communication with national competent authorities, other relevant authorities, including those providing or supporting access to data, notified bodies, other operators, customers, or other interested parties; (k) systems and procedures for record-keeping of all relevant documentation and information; (l) resource management, including supply-security related measures; (m) an accountability framework setting out the responsibilities of management and other staff with regard to all aspects listed in this paragraph. Art. 17(2) requires implementation of the aspects in paragraph 1 to be proportionate to the size of the provider's organisation, while maintaining the degree of stringency and level of protection required for compliance. Art. 17(3) allows providers subject to QMS obligations under other sectoral Union legislation to include the paragraph 1 aspects within those QMS. Art. 17(4) provides that for providers which are financial institutions subject to internal governance requirements under Union financial services law, the QMS obligation is deemed fulfilled — except for paragraph 1(g), (h), and (i) — when the internal governance rules and procedures pursuant to the relevant Union financial services law are complied with. The harmonised standards referred to in Art. 40 shall be taken into account for that purpose.
enforcementConsequence: No direct fine provision — violations sanctionable via Art. 16 (provider) umbrella obligations (Art. 99(4)(a): fines up to EUR 15 000 000 or 3%)

title: Documentation Retention
summary: Requires providers to retain technical documentation, QMS documentation, notified body decisions, and the EU declaration of conformity for 10 years after placing on the market or putting into service. Financial institution providers must maintain technical documentation as part of their financial services documentation obligations.
body: Art. 18(1) requires the provider to keep the following documentation available for national competent authorities for a period of 10 years from the placing on the market or putting into service of the high-risk AI system: (a) the technical documentation referred to in Art. 11; (b) the documentation concerning the quality management system referred to in Art. 17; (c) the documentation concerning changes approved by notified bodies, where applicable; (d) the decisions and other documents issued by the notified bodies, where applicable; (e) the EU declaration of conformity referred to in Art. 47. Art. 18(2) requires each Member State to determine the conditions under which the documentation in paragraph 1 remains available for national competent authorities for the period indicated, in the event that a provider or its authorised representative established in that territory goes bankrupt or ceases its activity before the end of that period. Art. 18(3) provides that providers which are financial institutions subject to internal governance requirements under Union financial services law shall maintain the technical documentation as part of the documentation kept under the relevant Union financial services law.
enforcementConsequence: No direct fine provision — violations sanctionable via Art. 16 (provider) umbrella obligations (Art. 99(4)(a): fines up to EUR 15 000 000 or 3%)

title: Automatically Generated Logs
summary: Requires providers to retain automatically generated logs per Art. 12(1) for a minimum of 6 months (unless other law requires longer), where under their control. Financial institution providers must keep logs as part of their financial services documentation.
body: Art. 19(1) requires providers of high-risk AI systems to keep the logs automatically generated by their high-risk AI systems as referred to in Art. 12(1), insofar as such logs are under their control. Without prejudice to applicable Union or national law, the logs shall be kept for a period appropriate to the intended purpose of the high-risk AI system, of at least six months, unless provided otherwise in applicable Union law, in particular Union law on the protection of personal data, or applicable national law. Art. 19(2) provides that providers which are financial institutions subject to internal governance requirements under Union financial services law shall maintain the logs automatically generated by their high-risk AI systems as part of the documentation kept under the relevant Union financial services law.
enforcementConsequence: No direct fine provision — violations sanctionable via Art. 16 (provider) umbrella obligations (Art. 99(4)(a): fines up to EUR 15 000 000 or 3%)

title: Corrective Actions and Duty of Information
summary: Requires providers who consider or have reason to believe their high-risk AI system does not conform to the Regulation to immediately take corrective measures (conformity restoration, withdrawal, deactivation, or recall) and inform distributors, deployers, authorised representatives, and importers. Providers must investigate risk causes and inform market surveillance authorities.
body: Art. 20(1) requires providers of high-risk AI systems who consider or have reason to believe that a high-risk AI system they have placed on the market or put into service is not in conformity with this Regulation to immediately take the necessary corrective measures to bring that system into conformity, to withdraw it, to disable it, or to recall it, as appropriate. They shall inform the distributors of the high-risk AI system concerned and, where applicable, the deployers, the authorised representative, and the importers accordingly. Art. 20(2) provides that where the high-risk AI system presents a risk within the meaning of Art. 79(1) and the provider becomes aware of that risk, it shall immediately, where applicable in cooperation with the reporting deployer, investigate the causes and inform the market surveillance authorities competent for the high-risk AI system concerned and, where applicable, the notified body that issued a certificate for that system in accordance with Art. 44, in particular about the nature of the non-conformity and about any relevant corrective measure already taken.
enforcementConsequence: No direct fine provision — violations sanctionable via Art. 16 (provider) umbrella obligations (Art. 99(4)(a): fines up to EUR 15 000 000 or 3%)

title: Cooperation with Competent Authorities
summary: Requires providers of high-risk AI systems to provide all information and documentation to competent authorities upon reasoned request, including access to automatically generated logs, in an official EU language. All information received is subject to confidentiality obligations per Art. 78.
body: Art. 21(1) requires providers of high-risk AI systems to submit to a competent authority, upon its reasoned request, all information and documentation necessary to demonstrate conformity of the high-risk AI system with the Section 2 requirements, in a language that is easily understandable to the authority and that is one of the official languages of the institutions of the Union indicated by the Member State concerned. Art. 21(2) requires providers, upon a reasoned request by a competent authority, to also grant that authority access to the automatically generated logs of the high-risk AI system referred to in Art. 12(1), insofar as such logs are under their control. Art. 21(3) provides that all information obtained by a competent authority pursuant to this Article shall be treated in accordance with the confidentiality obligations set out in Art. 78.
enforcementConsequence: No direct fine provision — violations sanctionable via Art. 16 (provider) umbrella obligations (Art. 99(4)(a): fines up to EUR 15 000 000 or 3%)

title: Authorised Representatives of Providers
summary: Requires third-country providers to appoint a written authorised representative in the Union before making high-risk AI systems available. The mandate must cover at minimum: verifying conformity documentation, retaining documentation for 10 years, providing information to authorities, cooperating with authorities, and ensuring registration compliance. The representative must terminate the mandate if the provider breaches its obligations.
body: Art. 22(1) requires providers established in third countries to designate, by written mandate, an authorised representative established in the Union before making their high-risk AI systems available on the Union market. Art. 22(2) requires the provider to enable its authorised representative to perform the tasks specified in the mandate received from the provider. Art. 22(3) requires the authorised representative to perform the tasks set out in the mandate. The representative shall provide the market surveillance authorities, on request, with a copy of the mandate in an official language of the institutions of the Union indicated by the competent authority. For the purposes of this Regulation, the mandate shall empower the authorised representative at least to: (a) verify that the EU declaration of conformity per Art. 47 and the technical documentation per Art. 11 have been drawn up and that the provider has carried out an appropriate conformity assessment procedure; (b) keep available — for 10 years from the placing on the market or putting into service — the contact details of the provider, a copy of the EU declaration of conformity, the technical documentation, and where applicable, the certificate issued by the notified body, for competent authorities and the national authorities or bodies referred to in Art. 74(10); (c) provide a competent authority, upon reasoned request, with all information and documentation necessary to demonstrate conformity, including access to the automatically generated logs per Art. 12(1) insofar as under the provider's control; (d) cooperate with competent authorities upon reasoned request on any action taken in connection with the high-risk AI system, in particular to reduce and mitigate risks; (e) where applicable, comply with the registration obligations under Art. 49(1) or ensure correctness of the information in Annex VIII Section A point 3. The mandate shall authorise the representative to serve as contact point for competent authorities alongside or instead of the provider on all matters concerning compliance with this Regulation. Art. 22(4) requires the authorised representative to terminate the mandate if it considers or has reason to consider that the provider acts contrary to its obligations under this Regulation, and to immediately inform the relevant market surveillance authority and, where applicable, the notified body about the termination and its reasons.
enforcementConsequence: Fines up to EUR 15 000 000 or 3% of total worldwide annual turnover (Art. 99(4)(b))

title: Obligations of Importers
summary: Requires importers to verify conformity (conformity assessment, technical documentation, CE marking, EU declaration, instructions for use, authorised representative) before placing a high-risk AI system on the market. Importers must label packaging, ensure storage/transport conditions, retain certificates for 10 years, provide information to authorities, and cooperate on risk mitigation.
body: Art. 23(1) requires importers, before placing a high-risk AI system on the market, to ensure conformity by verifying that: (a) the provider has carried out the appropriate conformity assessment procedure per Art. 43; (b) the provider has drawn up the technical documentation per Art. 11 and Annex IV; (c) the system bears the required CE marking and is accompanied by the EU declaration of conformity per Art. 47 and instructions for use; (d) the provider has appointed an authorised representative per Art. 22(1). Art. 23(2) provides that where an importer has sufficient reason to consider that a high-risk AI system is not in conformity or is falsified or accompanied by falsified documentation, it shall not place the system on the market until conformity has been established; where the system presents a risk per Art. 79(1), the importer shall inform the provider, authorised representatives, and market surveillance authorities. Art. 23(3) requires importers to indicate their name, registered trade name or trademark, and contact address on the packaging or, where applicable, the accompanying documentation. Art. 23(4) requires importers to ensure that, while the system is under their responsibility, storage or transport conditions do not jeopardise compliance with Section 2 requirements. Art. 23(5) requires importers to keep a copy of the notified body certificate, instructions for use, and the EU declaration of conformity per Art. 47 for 10 years. Art. 23(6) requires importers to provide all necessary information and documentation to national authorities upon reasoned request, in an easily understandable language, including making the technical documentation available. Art. 23(7) requires importers to cooperate with national authorities on all measures taken to reduce and mitigate risks.
enforcementConsequence: Fines up to EUR 15 000 000 or 3% of total worldwide annual turnover (Art. 99(4)(c))

title: Obligations of Distributors
summary: Requires distributors to verify CE marking, EU declaration of conformity, and instructions for use before making a high-risk AI system available on the market. Distributors must ensure proper storage/transport, take corrective measures for non-conforming systems, and cooperate with authorities.
body: Art. 24(1) requires distributors, before making a high-risk AI system available on the market, to verify that: the required CE marking is affixed; a copy of the EU declaration of conformity per Art. 47 and instructions for use are attached; and the provider and, where applicable, the importer have fulfilled their respective obligations under Art. 16(b) and (c) and Art. 23(3). Art. 24(2) provides that where a distributor considers or has reason to consider that a high-risk AI system is not in conformity with Section 2 requirements, it shall not make the system available until conformity has been established; where the system presents a risk per Art. 79(1), the distributor shall inform the provider or importer. Art. 24(3) requires distributors to ensure that, while the system is under their responsibility, storage or transport conditions do not jeopardise compliance with Section 2 requirements. Art. 24(4) requires a distributor who considers or has reason to consider that a system already made available is not in conformity to take corrective measures (conformity restoration, withdrawal, or recall) or ensure the provider, importer, or relevant operator takes them; where the system presents a risk per Art. 79(1), the distributor shall immediately inform the provider or importer and competent authorities, providing details on non-conformity and corrective measures. Art. 24(5) requires distributors to provide all necessary information and documentation on their measures under paragraphs 1-4 upon reasoned request. Art. 24(6) requires distributors to cooperate with competent authorities on all measures taken to reduce or mitigate risks.
enforcementConsequence: Fines up to EUR 15 000 000 or 3% of total worldwide annual turnover (Art. 99(4)(d))

title: Responsibilities Along the AI Value Chain
summary: Defines when distributors, importers, deployers, or third parties become providers subject to Art. 16 obligations: when they put their name/trademark on a system, make a substantial modification, or change the intended purpose so it becomes high-risk. Requires written agreements between providers and third-party component suppliers. Product manufacturers of safety-component AI are deemed providers.
body: Art. 25(1) provides that distributors, importers, deployers, or other third parties shall be considered providers of a high-risk AI system and subject to Art. 16 provider obligations in the following cases: (a) they put their name or trademark on a high-risk AI system already placed on the market or put into service, without prejudice to contractual arrangements providing for a different allocation of obligations; (b) they make a substantial modification to a high-risk AI system already placed on the market or put into service, so that it remains a high-risk AI system per Art. 6; (c) they modify the intended purpose of an AI system, including a general-purpose AI system not classified as high-risk, already placed on the market or put into service, so that it becomes a high-risk AI system per Art. 6. Art. 25(2) provides that under paragraph 1 circumstances, the original provider is no longer considered the provider for that specific AI system. The original provider shall cooperate closely with new providers, provide necessary information, and ensure reasonably expected technical access and other assistance needed for fulfilling Regulation obligations, in particular regarding conformity assessment. This does not apply where the original provider clearly specified that its AI system may not be converted into a high-risk AI system. Art. 25(3) provides that for high-risk AI systems that are safety components of products under Annex I Section A harmonisation legislation, the product manufacturer is deemed the provider and subject to Art. 16 obligations when: (a) the high-risk AI system is placed on the market together with the product under the manufacturer's name or trademark; (b) the high-risk AI system is put into service under the manufacturer's name or trademark after the product has been placed on the market. Art. 25(4) requires the provider of a high-risk AI system and the third party supplying AI systems, tools, services, components, or processes used in or integrated into a high-risk AI system to set out in a written agreement the information, capabilities, technical access, and other assistance needed for the provider to fully comply with this Regulation. This does not apply to third parties making tools, services, processes, or components (other than general-purpose AI models) publicly available under a free and open-source licence. The AI Office may develop and recommend voluntary model terms for such contracts. Art. 25(5) preserves the need to respect intellectual property rights, confidential business information, and trade secrets.
enforcementConsequence: No direct fine provision — new provider status triggers Art. 16 obligations (Art. 99(4)(a): fines up to EUR 15 000 000 or 3%)

title: Obligations of Deployers of High-Risk AI Systems
summary: Central deployer obligation provision with 12 paragraphs: use per instructions, assign qualified human oversight, ensure appropriate input data, monitor operation and report risks/incidents, retain logs for min. 6 months, inform workers, register (EU institutions), use information for DPIA, obtain judicial authorisation for post-remote biometric identification, inform affected persons, and cooperate with authorities. Financial institutions may fulfil monitoring and log retention obligations through existing internal governance procedures.
body: Art. 26(1) requires deployers to take appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure they use high-risk AI systems in accordance with the instructions for use and in accordance with paragraphs 3 and 6. Art. 26(2) requires deployers to assign human oversight to natural persons who have the necessary competence, training, and authority, and to provide them with the necessary support. Art. 26(3) preserves other deployer obligations under Union or national law and the deployer's freedom to organise its own resources and activities for implementing the provider's human oversight measures. Art. 26(4) requires deployers, insofar as input data are under their control, to ensure that input data are relevant to the intended purpose and sufficiently representative. Art. 26(5) requires deployers to monitor the operation of the high-risk AI system on the basis of the instructions for use and to inform providers per Art. 72 where applicable. Where deployers have reason to consider that use in accordance with the instructions may result in a risk per Art. 79(1), they shall immediately inform the provider or distributor and the competent market surveillance authority and suspend use. Where deployers have identified a serious incident, they shall also immediately inform the provider and then the importer or distributor and competent market surveillance authorities. Where the deployer cannot reach the provider, Art. 73 applies mutatis mutandis. This obligation does not apply to sensitive operational data of deployers that are law enforcement authorities. For deployers which are financial institutions subject to internal governance requirements under Union financial services law, the monitoring obligation under subparagraph 1 is deemed fulfilled when the rules on internal governance arrangements, processes, or mechanisms pursuant to the relevant financial services law are complied with. Art. 26(6) requires deployers to keep the automatically generated logs for a period appropriate to the intended purpose of at least six months, unless otherwise provided by applicable Union or national law. For deployers which are financial institutions subject to internal governance requirements, the logs shall be kept as part of the documentation under the relevant Union financial services law. Art. 26(7) requires deployers that are employers to inform worker representatives and affected workers before putting into service or using a high-risk AI system at the workplace, in accordance with applicable Union and national rules on worker information. Art. 26(8) requires deployers that are Union institutions, bodies, offices, or agencies to comply with Art. 49 registration obligations; if they find the system is not registered in the EU database per Art. 71, they shall refrain from using it and inform the provider or distributor. Art. 26(9) requires deployers to use the information provided per Art. 13 to comply with their obligation to carry out a data protection impact assessment per Art. 35 GDPR or Art. 27 Directive 2016/680, where applicable. Art. 26(10) requires deployers of post-remote biometric identification systems for law enforcement to seek prior or prompt judicial or administrative authorisation (within 48 hours), with restrictions on untargeted use, prohibition of decisions based solely on system output, documentation requirements, annual reporting, and Member State authority to adopt stricter rules. Art. 26(11) requires deployers of Annex III high-risk AI systems that make or support decisions concerning natural persons to inform those persons that they are subject to the use of the system; for law enforcement purposes, Art. 13 of Directive 2016/680 applies. Art. 26(12) requires deployers to cooperate with competent authorities on all measures those authorities take in connection with the high-risk AI system.
enforcementConsequence: Fines up to EUR 15 000 000 or 3% of total worldwide annual turnover (Art. 99(4)(e))

title: Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment for High-Risk AI Systems
summary: Requires public law bodies, private entities providing public services, and deployers of Annex III No. 5(b) and (c) systems to conduct a fundamental rights impact assessment (FRIA) before putting a high-risk AI system into service. The FRIA must cover: processes, frequency of use, affected person categories, specific harm risks, human oversight implementation, and risk response measures. Results must be notified to the market surveillance authority.
body: Art. 27(1) requires deployers that are bodies governed by public law or private entities providing public services, and deployers of high-risk AI systems referred to in Annex III point 5(b) and (c), before putting into service a high-risk AI system under Art. 6(2) — except systems intended to be used in the area listed in Annex III point 2 — to perform an assessment of the impact that the use of such a system may have on fundamental rights. The assessment shall comprise: (a) a description of the deployer's processes in which the high-risk AI system will be used in line with its intended purpose; (b) a description of the period of time within which, and the frequency with which, each high-risk AI system is intended to be used; (c) the categories of natural persons and groups of persons likely to be affected by its use in the specific context; (d) the specific risks of harm likely to impact the categories identified under (c), taking into account the information provided by the provider per Art. 13; (e) a description of the implementation of human oversight measures, in accordance with the instructions for use; (f) the measures to be taken in the case of materialisation of those risks, including the arrangements for internal governance and complaint mechanisms. Art. 27(2) provides that the obligation applies to the first use of a high-risk AI system. The deployer may rely in similar cases on previously conducted FRIAs or on existing impact assessments carried out by the provider. If the deployer considers during use that any of the paragraph 1 elements has changed or is no longer up to date, it shall take the necessary steps to update the information. Art. 27(3) requires the deployer, once the assessment has been performed, to notify the market surveillance authority of the results by submitting the completed template referred to in paragraph 5 as part of the notification. Deployers may be exempt from the notification obligation in the case referred to in Art. 46(1). Art. 27(4) provides that where an obligation under this Article is already fulfilled as a result of a data protection impact assessment per Art. 35 GDPR or Art. 27 Directive 2016/680, the fundamental rights impact assessment shall complement that data protection impact assessment. Art. 27(5) requires the AI Office to develop a template for a questionnaire, including through an automated tool, to enable deployers to comply with their obligations under this Article in a simplified manner.
enforcementConsequence: No direct fine provision — deployer obligation sanctionable via Art. 26 umbrella (Art. 99(4)(e): fines up to EUR 15 000 000 or 3%)

title: Harmonised Standards and Standardisation Deliverables
summary: Establishes the presumption of conformity for high-risk AI systems or GPAI models that comply with harmonised standards published in the Official Journal. Requires the Commission to issue standardisation requests covering all Section 2 requirements, including energy efficiency reporting. Standards must be clear, consistent with sector-specific standards, and ensure compliance.
body: Art. 40(1) provides that high-risk AI systems or general-purpose AI models that are in conformity with harmonised standards or parts thereof, the references of which have been published in the Official Journal of the European Union in accordance with Regulation (EU) No 1025/2012, shall be presumed to be in conformity with the Section 2 requirements of this Chapter or, where applicable, the obligations under Chapter V Sections 2 and 3, to the extent those requirements or obligations are covered by those standards. Art. 40(2) requires the Commission, pursuant to Art. 10 of Regulation (EU) No 1025/2012, to issue without undue delay standardisation requests covering all Section 2 requirements and, where applicable, obligations under Chapter V Sections 2 and 3. The standardisation requests shall also require deliverables on reporting and documentation processes aimed at improving AI system resource performance, such as reducing energy and other resource consumption throughout the lifecycle, and on energy-efficient development of general-purpose AI models. The Commission shall consult the AI Board and relevant stakeholders, including the Advisory Forum, when preparing the request. When issuing the request, the Commission shall specify that the standards must be clear, consistent (including with standards developed in various sectors for products under Annex I harmonisation legislation), and ensure that high-risk AI systems or GPAI models placed on the market or put into service comply with the relevant requirements or obligations. The Commission shall request the European standardisation organisations to provide evidence of their best efforts to achieve these objectives per Art. 24 of Regulation (EU) No 1025/2012. Art. 40(3) requires standardisation process participants to endeavour to promote investment and innovation in AI, competitiveness and growth of the Union market, to contribute to strengthening global cooperation on standardisation, to account for existing international AI standards consistent with Union values, fundamental rights, and interests, and to improve multi-stakeholder governance by ensuring balanced representation and effective participation of all relevant stakeholders per Articles 5, 6, and 7 of Regulation (EU) No 1025/2012.
enforcementConsequence: No direct fine provision — framework provision establishing presumption of conformity

title: Common Specifications
summary: Empowers the Commission to adopt implementing acts establishing common specifications where harmonised standards are absent, rejected, insufficient for fundamental rights, or non-conforming. Compliance with common specifications establishes a presumption of conformity. Providers not following common specifications must demonstrate equivalent technical solutions.
body: Art. 41(1) empowers the Commission to adopt implementing acts laying down common specifications for Section 2 requirements or Chapter V Sections 2 and 3 obligations where: (a) the Commission has mandated European standardisation organisations under Art. 10(1) of Regulation (EU) No 1025/2012 and either (i) no organisation accepted the mandate, (ii) harmonised standards were not delivered within the deadline, (iii) the standards do not sufficiently address fundamental rights concerns, or (iv) the standards do not correspond to the mandate; and (b) no harmonised standard references have been published in the Official Journal, and none are expected to be published within a reasonable period. The Commission shall consult the Advisory Forum per Art. 67. Implementing acts shall be adopted per the examination procedure in Art. 98(2). Art. 41(2) requires the Commission, before preparing a draft implementing act, to inform the committee referred to in Art. 22 of Regulation (EU) No 1025/2012 that it considers the paragraph 1 conditions fulfilled. Art. 41(3) provides a presumption of conformity for high-risk AI systems or GPAI models conforming to the common specifications, to the extent covered. Art. 41(4) provides that when a harmonised standard is adopted and proposed for publication, the Commission shall assess it; if the reference is published, the implementing acts covering the same requirements shall be wholly or partially repealed. Art. 41(5) requires providers not following common specifications to demonstrate that their technical solutions meet the requirements at least to an equivalent degree. Art. 41(6) allows Member States to notify the Commission if a common specification does not fully meet the requirements, upon which the Commission shall assess and amend if appropriate.
enforcementConsequence: No direct fine provision — framework provision establishing presumption of conformity

title: Presumption of Conformity with Certain Requirements
summary: Establishes two specific presumptions of conformity: (1) high-risk AI systems trained and tested with data reflecting their specific deployment context are presumed to meet Art. 10(4) data requirements; (2) high-risk AI systems certified under an EU Cybersecurity Act certification scheme are presumed to meet Art. 15 cybersecurity requirements, insofar as covered.
