body: Art. 42(1) provides that high-risk AI systems that have been trained and tested on data reflecting the specific geographical, behavioural, contextual, or functional setting within which they are intended to be used shall be presumed to be in compliance with the relevant requirements laid down in Art. 10(4). Art. 42(2) provides that high-risk AI systems that have been certified or for which a statement of conformity has been issued under a cybersecurity scheme pursuant to Regulation (EU) 2019/881, the references of which have been published in the Official Journal of the European Union, shall be presumed to be in compliance with the cybersecurity requirements set out in Art. 15 of this Regulation, insofar as those requirements are covered by the cybersecurity certification or statement of conformity or parts thereof.
enforcementConsequence: No direct fine provision — presumption of conformity mechanism

title: Conformity Assessment
summary: Defines conformity assessment procedures for high-risk AI systems. Annex III No. 1 systems: choice between internal control (Annex VI) or notified body assessment (Annex VII) when harmonised standards applied; mandatory Annex VII procedure otherwise. Annex III Nos. 2-8: internal control only. Annex I Section A products: follow the sectoral conformity assessment. Substantial modifications require re-assessment.
body: Art. 43(1) provides that for Annex III point 1 high-risk AI systems where the provider has applied harmonised standards per Art. 40 or common specifications per Art. 41, the provider may choose between: (a) internal control per Annex VI; or (b) assessment of the quality management system and technical documentation with the involvement of a notified body per Annex VII. Where harmonised standards do not exist or common specifications are not available, the provider has not applied or only partially applied them, the standards were published with a restriction, the provider must follow the Annex VII procedure. For Annex VII procedures, the provider may select a notified body; however, where the system is to be put into service by law enforcement, immigration or asylum authorities or EU institutions, the market surveillance authority referred to in Art. 74(8) or (9) shall act as the notified body. Art. 43(2) provides that for Annex III points 2 to 8 high-risk AI systems, providers shall follow the internal control conformity assessment procedure per Annex VI, which does not involve a notified body. Art. 43(3) provides that for high-risk AI systems covered by Annex I Section A Union harmonisation legislation, providers shall follow the relevant conformity assessment procedures under those acts; Section 2 requirements apply and are integrated into the assessment; Annex VII points 4.3, 4.4, 4.5, and point 4.6 paragraph 5 also apply. Notified bodies under those acts may control AI Act compliance if verified during notified body designation. Where the sectoral legislation permits waiver of third-party assessment if all harmonised standards are applied, the manufacturer may only do so if it also applied harmonised standards or common specifications covering all Section 2 requirements. Art. 43(4) requires high-risk AI systems that have already undergone conformity assessment to undergo a new procedure in case of a substantial modification, regardless of whether the modified system is to remain on the market or continue to be used. For continuously learning systems, changes pre-determined by the provider at the time of the original assessment and documented in Annex IV point 2(f) technical documentation do not constitute a substantial modification. Art. 43(5) empowers the Commission to adopt delegated acts per Art. 97 to update Annexes VI and VII. Art. 43(6) empowers the Commission to adopt delegated acts to subject Annex III points 2-8 systems to the Annex VII procedure, considering effectiveness of internal control, availability of notified body resources.
enforcementConsequence: No direct fine provision — violations sanctionable via Art. 16 (provider) umbrella obligations (Art. 99(4)(a): fines up to EUR 15 000 000 or 3%)

title: EU Declaration of Conformity
summary: Requires providers to draw up a written, machine-readable, signed EU declaration of conformity for each high-risk AI system, kept available for 10 years. The declaration must state Section 2 compliance, contain Annex V information, and be translated into an easily understandable language for the relevant Member States. A single declaration covers multiple applicable Union acts.
body: Art. 47(1) requires the provider to draw up a written machine-readable, physically or electronically signed EU declaration of conformity for each high-risk AI system and keep it available for national competent authorities for a period of 10 years from the placing on the market or putting into service. The declaration shall identify the high-risk AI system for which it was drawn up. A copy shall be submitted to the competent national authorities upon request. Art. 47(2) requires the EU declaration of conformity to state that the high-risk AI system fulfils the Section 2 requirements, contain the information set out in Annex V, and be translated into a language easily understandable for the competent national authorities of the Member States in which the system is placed on the market or made available. Art. 47(3) provides that where high-risk AI systems are subject to other Union harmonisation legislation also requiring an EU declaration of conformity, a single EU declaration shall be drawn up covering all applicable Union legislation, containing all required information for identifying the applicable harmonisation legislation. Art. 47(4) provides that by drawing up the EU declaration of conformity, the provider assumes responsibility for compliance with the Section 2 requirements and shall keep the declaration up to date as appropriate. Art. 47(5) empowers the Commission to adopt delegated acts per Art. 97 to update the content of the EU declaration of conformity in Annex V as necessary in light of technical progress.
enforcementConsequence: No direct fine provision — violations sanctionable via Art. 16 (provider) umbrella obligations (Art. 99(4)(a): fines up to EUR 15 000 000 or 3%)

title: CE Marking
summary: Applies the general principles of CE marking per Regulation (EC) No 765/2008 to high-risk AI systems. Requires visible, legible, and indelible affixing of the CE marking, with provisions for digital systems. The notified body identification number must be added where applicable.
body: Art. 48(1) provides that the general principles of CE marking set out in Art. 30 of Regulation (EC) No 765/2008 apply to the CE marking. Art. 48(2) provides that for digitally provided high-risk AI systems, a digital CE marking shall only be used if it is easily accessible through the interface from which the system is accessed, or via an easily accessible machine-readable code or other electronic means. Art. 48(3) requires the CE marking to be affixed visibly, legibly, and indelibly to the high-risk AI system; where the nature of the system does not permit or warrant this, it shall be affixed to the packaging or the accompanying documentation. Art. 48(4) requires the identification number of the notified body responsible for the Art. 43 conformity assessment procedures to be added to the CE marking where applicable; the number shall be affixed by the body itself or by the provider or its authorised representative following the body's instructions, and shall also appear on any promotional material indicating that the system meets the CE marking requirements. Art. 48(5) provides that where high-risk AI systems are also subject to other Union legislation providing for the CE marking, the CE marking indicates that the system also fulfils the requirements of that other legislation.
enforcementConsequence: No direct fine provision — violations sanctionable via Art. 16 (provider) umbrella obligations (Art. 99(4)(a): fines up to EUR 15 000 000 or 3%)

title: Registration
summary: Requires registration in the EU database (Art. 71) before placing on the market or putting into service: providers of Annex III high-risk AI systems (except Annex III No. 2), providers concluding systems are not high-risk under Art. 6(3), and public authority deployers. Law enforcement, migration, asylum, and border control systems are registered in a secure non-public section. Annex III No. 2 systems are registered at national level.
body: Art. 49(1) requires the provider or, where applicable, its authorised representative, before placing on the market or putting into service a high-risk AI system listed in Annex III — except those referred to in Annex III point 2 — to register itself and its system in the EU database referred to in Art. 71. Art. 49(2) requires providers who have concluded that their system is not high-risk under Art. 6(3) to register themselves and the system in the EU database before placing on the market or putting into service. Art. 49(3) requires deployers that are public authorities or entities acting on their behalf, or Union institutions, bodies, offices, or agencies, before putting into service or using an Annex III high-risk AI system (except Annex III point 2), to register in the EU database and select and register the system. Art. 49(4) provides that for Annex III points 1, 6, and 7 high-risk AI systems in the areas of law enforcement, migration, asylum, and border control, registration under paragraphs 1, 2, and 3 is done in a secure non-public section of the EU database, containing only the information per: (a) Annex VIII Section A points 1-10 except 6, 8, and 9; (b) Annex VIII Section B points 1-5 and 8-9; (c) Annex VIII Section C points 1-3; (d) Annex IX points 1, 2, 3, and 5. Only the Commission and the national authorities referred to in Art. 74(8) have access to the restricted sections. Art. 49(5) provides that Annex III point 2 high-risk AI systems are registered at national level.
enforcementConsequence: No direct fine provision — violations sanctionable via Art. 16 (provider) or Art. 26 (deployer) umbrella obligations

title: Transparency Obligations for Providers and Deployers of Certain AI Systems
summary: Establishes transparency obligations for specific AI system categories: (1) providers of human-interacting AI must disclose AI nature; (2) providers of synthetic content systems must ensure machine-readable labelling; (3) deployers of emotion recognition or biometric categorisation must inform affected persons; (4) deployers of deepfake systems must disclose artificial generation/manipulation. Information must be provided clearly at the latest upon first interaction.
body: Art. 50(1) requires providers to ensure that AI systems intended for direct interaction with natural persons are designed and developed so that the persons are informed they are interacting with an AI system, unless this is obvious from the circumstances and context of use to a reasonably informed, attentive, and circumspect natural person. This does not apply to AI systems authorised by law for detection, prevention, investigation, or prosecution of criminal offences, with appropriate safeguards for third-party rights, unless those systems are available to the public for reporting offences. Art. 50(2) requires providers of AI systems, including general-purpose AI systems, that generate synthetic audio, image, video, or text content to ensure that the outputs are marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated. Providers shall ensure, where technically feasible, that their technical solutions are effective, interoperable, robust, and reliable, having regard to content type specificities, implementation costs, and state of the art. This does not apply where systems perform an assistive function for standard editing or do not substantially alter the input data or its semantics, or where authorised for criminal offence detection/prevention/investigation/prosecution. Art. 50(3) requires deployers of emotion recognition systems or biometric categorisation systems to inform the affected natural persons of the system's operation and to process personal data per Regulations 2016/679 and 2018/1725 and Directive 2016/680. This does not apply to AI systems authorised for criminal offence detection, prevention, or investigation, with appropriate safeguards. Art. 50(4) requires deployers of AI systems generating or manipulating image, audio, or video content constituting a deep fake to disclose that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated. This does not apply where authorised for criminal offence detection/prevention/investigation/prosecution. For obviously artistic, creative, satirical, fictional or analogous works, disclosure must be made in an appropriate manner that does not impair the display or enjoyment of the work. Deployers of AI systems generating or manipulating text that is published to inform the public on matters of public interest must disclose the artificial generation or manipulation; this does not apply where authorised for law enforcement or where AI-generated content has undergone human review or editorial control and a natural or legal person bears editorial responsibility. Art. 50(5) requires the information under paragraphs 1-4 to be provided clearly and distinguishably at the latest at the time of first interaction or exposure, and to comply with applicable accessibility requirements. Art. 50(6) preserves Chapter III requirements and obligations and does not affect other Union or national law transparency obligations. Art. 50(7) requires the AI Office to promote and facilitate codes of practice at Union level for content labelling and detection; the Commission may adopt implementing acts to approve such codes or, if inadequate, lay down common rules.
enforcementConsequence: Fines up to EUR 15 000 000 or 3% of total worldwide annual turnover (Art. 99(4)(g))

title: Classification of General-Purpose AI Models as Systemic Risk Models
summary: Defines when a GPAI model is classified as having systemic risk: (1) high-impact capabilities assessed through technical tools/benchmarks, or (2) Commission decision ex officio or following a qualified alert from the scientific panel. A model is presumed to have high-impact capabilities when cumulative training compute exceeds 10^25 FLOPs. Commission may amend thresholds via delegated acts.
body: Art. 51(1) provides that a general-purpose AI model shall be classified as a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk if either of the following conditions is met: (a) it has high-impact capabilities evaluated on the basis of appropriate technical tools and methodologies, including indicators and benchmarks; (b) based on a decision of the Commission, taking into account the criteria set out in Annex XIII, ex officio or following a qualified alert from the scientific panel, it has capabilities or an impact equivalent to those under (a). Art. 51(2) provides that a GPAI model shall be presumed to have high-impact capabilities per paragraph 1(a) when the cumulative amount of computation used for its training, measured in floating point operations, is greater than 10^25. Art. 51(3) empowers the Commission to adopt delegated acts per Art. 97 to amend the thresholds in paragraphs 1 and 2 and to supplement benchmarks and indicators in light of evolving technological developments, such as algorithmic improvements or increased hardware efficiency, to ensure those thresholds reflect the state of the art.
enforcementConsequence: No direct fine provision — classification mechanism triggering Art. 55 obligations

title: Obligations for Providers of General-Purpose AI Models
summary: Requires GPAI model providers to: (a) prepare and maintain technical documentation (Annex XI); (b) provide information and documentation to downstream AI system providers (Annex XII); (c) implement a copyright compliance policy including for Art. 4(3) Directive 2019/790 opt-outs; (d) publish a detailed training content summary per AI Office template. Open-source model providers are exempt from (a) and (b) unless systemic risk. Providers may rely on codes of practice or harmonised standards for compliance.
body: Art. 53(1) requires providers of general-purpose AI models to: (a) draw up and keep up to date the technical documentation of the model, including its training and testing process and evaluation results, containing at least the information set out in Annex XI, to be made available on request to the AI Office and national competent authorities; (b) draw up, keep up to date, and make available information and documentation to providers of AI systems that intend to integrate the GPAI model, without prejudice to intellectual property rights and confidential business information, such information and documentation must (i) enable AI system providers to understand the capabilities and limitations of the GPAI model and comply with their obligations under this Regulation, and (ii) contain at least the elements referred to in Annex XII; (c) put in place a policy to comply with Union copyright law and related rights, in particular to identify and comply with a reservation of rights expressed pursuant to Art. 4(3) of Directive (EU) 2019/790, including through state-of-the-art technologies; (d) draw up and make publicly available a sufficiently detailed summary of the content used for training the GPAI model, according to a template provided by the AI Office. Art. 53(2) exempts providers of GPAI models released under a free and open-source licence that allows access, use, modification, and distribution, and whose parameters including weights, model architecture information, and model usage information are made publicly available, from the obligations in paragraph 1(a) and (b). This exemption does not apply to GPAI models with systemic risks. Art. 53(3) requires GPAI model providers to cooperate as necessary with the Commission and national competent authorities in the exercise of their competences and powers under this Regulation. Art. 53(4) allows GPAI model providers to rely on codes of practice per Art. 56 until a harmonised standard is published to demonstrate compliance. Compliance with a harmonised European standard gives providers a presumption of conformity insofar as those standards cover the obligations. Providers not following an approved code or not complying with a harmonised standard must demonstrate appropriate alternative means of compliance for Commission assessment. Art. 53(5) empowers the Commission to adopt delegated acts per Art. 97 to specify measurement and calculation methodologies for Annex XI, particularly point 2(d) and (e), to enable comparable and verifiable documentation. Art. 53(6) empowers the Commission to adopt delegated acts to amend Annexes XI and XII in light of technological developments. Art. 53(7) provides that all information or documentation obtained under this Article shall be treated in accordance with the confidentiality obligations in Art. 78.
enforcementConsequence: Enforced by the Commission via Art. 101 — fines up to EUR 15 000 000 or 3% of total worldwide annual turnover

title: Obligations for Providers of General-Purpose AI Models with Systemic Risk
summary: Requires GPAI models classified as systemic risk (in addition to Art. 53 and 54 obligations) to: (a) perform model evaluation including adversarial testing; (b) assess and mitigate possible systemic risks at Union level; (c) track, document, and report serious incidents to the AI Office; (d) ensure adequate cybersecurity for the model and physical infrastructure. Providers may rely on codes of practice or harmonised standards.
body: Art. 55(1) requires providers of general-purpose AI models with systemic risk, in addition to the obligations listed in Articles 53 and 54, to: (a) perform model evaluation with standardised protocols and tools reflecting the state of the art, including conducting and documenting adversarial testing of the model to identify and mitigate systemic risks; (b) assess and mitigate possible systemic risks at Union level, including their sources, that may stem from the development, the placing on the market, or the use of GPAI models with systemic risk; (c) keep track of, document, and report relevant information about serious incidents and possible corrective measures to the AI Office and, where appropriate, to national competent authorities, without undue delay; (d) ensure an adequate level of cybersecurity protection for the GPAI model with systemic risk and the physical infrastructure of the model. Art. 55(2) allows providers to rely on codes of practice per Art. 56 until a harmonised standard is published to demonstrate compliance. Compliance with a harmonised European standard gives a presumption of conformity. Providers not following an approved code or not complying with a harmonised standard must demonstrate appropriate alternative means of compliance for Commission assessment. Art. 55(3) provides that all information or documentation obtained under this Article shall be treated in accordance with the confidentiality obligations in Art. 78.
enforcementConsequence: Enforced by the Commission via Art. 101 — fines up to EUR 15 000 000 or 3% of total worldwide annual turnover

title: Real-World Testing of High-Risk AI Systems Outside AI Regulatory Sandboxes
summary: Permits providers or prospective providers of Annex III high-risk AI systems to conduct real-world testing outside regulatory sandboxes, subject to 11 conditions including: a testing plan approved by the market surveillance authority, EU database registration, Union establishment, data transfer safeguards, max 6-month duration (extendable), protection of vulnerable groups, informed consent, qualified oversight, and reversibility of outputs. Serious incidents must be reported per Art. 73.
body: Art. 60(1) permits real-world testing of Annex III high-risk AI systems by providers or prospective providers outside AI regulatory sandboxes in accordance with this Article and a real-world testing plan, without prejudice to Art. 5. The Commission shall lay down the elements of the testing plan by implementing acts. Union or national law for testing in connection with Annex I harmonisation legislation products is unaffected. Art. 60(2) permits providers or prospective providers to test Annex III high-risk AI systems under real-world conditions at any time before placing on the market or putting into service, alone or in partnership with deployers or prospective deployers. Art. 60(3) preserves ethics reviews required by Union or national law. Art. 60(4) requires the following conditions to be met: (a) the provider has drawn up a testing plan and submitted it to the market surveillance authority in the relevant Member State; (b) the market surveillance authority has approved the test and plan (deemed approved if no response within 30 days, unless national law requires explicit approval); (c) registration in the EU database per Art. 71(4) with a unique Union-wide identification number and Annex IX information (with secure non-public registration for law enforcement/migration/asylum/border systems per Art. 49(4)(d), and national registration for Annex III point 2 systems); (d) the provider is established in the Union or has appointed a legal representative; (e) data collected is only transferred to third countries where appropriate Union law safeguards apply; (f) duration does not exceed 6 months, extendable by further 6 months with prior notification and explanation; (g) vulnerable testing subjects (age, disability) are adequately protected; (h) where organised with deployers, all parties are informed and provided Art. 13 instructions for use, and a written agreement on roles and responsibilities is concluded; (i) informed consent per Art. 61, or where in law enforcement consent would prevent the test, the test must not negatively affect subjects and their personal data are deleted after the test; (j) testing is effectively supervised by adequately qualified persons with necessary ability, training, and authority; (k) predictions, recommendations, or decisions of the AI system can be effectively reversed and disregarded. Art. 60(5) guarantees test subjects the right to withdraw consent at any time and request immediate permanent deletion of personal data without detriment. Art. 60(6) requires Member States to empower market surveillance authorities to require information, conduct unannounced inspections, and check tests and related high-risk AI systems. Art. 60(7) requires serious incidents to be reported per Art. 73; the provider must take immediate mitigation measures or suspend/terminate the test and establish a recall procedure. Art. 60(8) requires notification to the market surveillance authority of suspension, termination, and final results. Art. 60(9) provides that providers remain liable for damages under applicable Union and national law.
enforcementConsequence: No direct fine provision — violations may be sanctionable via Art. 16 (provider) umbrella obligations

title: EU Database for High-Risk AI Systems Listed in Annex III
summary: Requires the Commission to establish and maintain an EU database for Annex III high-risk AI systems registered under Art. 49 and 60, and systems classified as non-high-risk under Art. 6(3). Provider/authorised representative data entered per Annex VIII Sections A and B; deployer data per Section C. Information is publicly accessible and machine-readable (except secure law enforcement sections). The Commission is data controller.
body: Art. 71(1) requires the Commission, in cooperation with the Member States, to set up and maintain an EU database containing the information referred to in paragraphs 2 and 3 concerning high-risk AI systems per Art. 6(2) registered under Art. 49 and 60, and AI systems not classified as high-risk per Art. 6(3) registered under Art. 6(4) and Art. 49. The Commission shall consult relevant experts for functional specifications and the AI Board for updates. Art. 71(2) requires the data listed in Annex VIII Sections A and B to be entered into the EU database by the provider or, where applicable, the authorised representative. Art. 71(3) requires the data listed in Annex VIII Section C to be entered by the deployer that is an authority, body, or entity, or acting on their behalf, in accordance with Art. 49(3) and (4). Art. 71(4) provides that, except for the sections referred to in Art. 49(4) and Art. 60(4)(c), the information registered under Art. 49 must be accessible and publicly available in a user-friendly manner, be easily navigable, and be machine-readable. Information registered under Art. 60 is accessible only to market surveillance authorities and the Commission, unless the prospective or actual provider has consented to public access. Art. 71(5) limits personal data in the EU database to what is necessary, including names and contact details of the natural persons responsible for registration and legally authorised to represent the provider or deployer. Art. 71(6) designates the Commission as the data controller; it shall provide adequate technical and administrative support to providers, prospective providers, and deployers; the database must comply with applicable accessibility requirements.
enforcementConsequence: No direct fine provision — institutional framework provision

title: Post-Market Monitoring by Providers and Post-Market Monitoring Plan for High-Risk AI Systems
summary: Requires providers of high-risk AI systems to establish and document a post-market monitoring system proportionate to the nature of the AI technology and risks, based on a post-market monitoring plan that forms part of the technical documentation under Annex IV.
body: Art. 72(1) requires providers to establish and document a post-market monitoring system proportionate to the nature of the AI technology and the risks of the high-risk AI system. Art. 72(2) provides that the post-market monitoring system shall actively and systematically collect, document, and analyse relevant data on the performance of high-risk AI systems throughout their lifetime, as provided by providers or deployers or collected from other sources, enabling the provider to evaluate the continuous compliance of AI systems with the requirements set out in Chapter III Section 2. Where relevant, post-market monitoring shall include an analysis of the interaction with other AI systems. This obligation does not apply to sensitive operational data of deployers that are law enforcement authorities. Art. 72(3) states that the post-market monitoring system shall be based on a post-market monitoring plan. The post-market monitoring plan shall be part of the technical documentation referred to in Annex IV. The Commission shall adopt an implementing act laying down detailed provisions establishing a template for the post-market monitoring plan and the list of elements to be included in the plan by 2 February 2026. Art. 72(4) provides that for high-risk AI systems covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I Section A, where a post-market monitoring system and plan have already been established under that legislation, providers may integrate the required elements referred to in paragraphs (1), (2) and (3) into the existing systems and plans, using the template referred to in paragraph (3), provided that an equivalent level of protection is achieved. Subparagraph 1 of this paragraph also applies to high-risk AI systems referred to in Annex III point 5 placed on the market or put into service by financial institutions that are subject to requirements regarding their internal governance, arrangements or processes under Union financial services law.
enforcementConsequence: Art. 99(4): up to EUR 15 000 000 or 3% of worldwide annual turnover (via Art. 16 provider obligations)

title: Reporting of Serious Incidents
summary: Obliges providers of high-risk AI systems placed on the Union market to report serious incidents to the market surveillance authorities of the Member State where the incident occurred, with specific timelines depending on severity (15 days general, 2 days for widespread infringements, immediate for death).
body: Art. 73(1) requires providers of high-risk AI systems placed on the Union market to report serious incidents to the market surveillance authorities of the Member States in which the incident occurred. Art. 73(2) provides that the report referred to in paragraph (1) shall be made immediately after the provider has established a causal link between the AI system and the serious incident or the reasonable likelihood of such a link, and in any event not later than 15 days after the provider or, where applicable, the deployer becomes aware of the serious incident. The reporting period shall take into account the severity of the serious incident. Art. 73(3) provides that notwithstanding paragraph (2), in the case of a widespread infringement or a serious incident as defined in Art. 3(49)(b), the report shall be made immediately and not later than two days after the provider or the deployer becomes aware of the incident. Art. 73(4) provides that notwithstanding paragraph (2), in the case of the death of a person, the report shall be made immediately after the provider or the deployer has established, or suspects, a causal link between the high-risk AI system and the serious incident, but not later than 10 days after the date on which the provider or the deployer becomes aware of the serious incident. Art. 73(5) allows the provider or deployer to submit an incomplete initial report followed by a complete report where necessary to ensure timely reporting. Art. 73(6) requires that following a report of a serious incident pursuant to paragraph (1), the provider shall without delay carry out the necessary investigations in relation to the serious incident and the AI system concerned, including a risk assessment of the incident and corrective action. The provider shall cooperate with the competent authorities and the relevant notified body, and shall not carry out any investigation that would lead to a modification of the AI system in a way that may affect any subsequent evaluation of the causes without first informing the competent authorities. Art. 73(7) provides that upon receipt of a report relating to a serious incident referred to in Art. 3(49)(c), the competent market surveillance authority shall inform the national authorities or public bodies referred to in Art. 77(1). The Commission shall develop dedicated guidance by 2 August 2025. Art. 73(8) requires the market surveillance authority to take appropriate measures in accordance with Art. 19 of Regulation (EU) 2019/1020 within seven days of receiving the report. Art. 73(9) provides that for high-risk AI systems listed in Annex III placed on the market or put into service by providers subject to Union legal instruments imposing reporting obligations equivalent to those set out in this Regulation, only serious incidents referred to in Art. 3(49)(c) need to be reported. Art. 73(10) provides that for high-risk AI systems that are safety components of devices or are themselves devices covered by Regulations (EU) 2017/745 and (EU) 2017/746, only serious incidents referred to in Art. 3(49)(c) shall be reported to the relevant competent national authority. Art. 73(11) requires competent national authorities to notify the Commission without delay of any serious incident in accordance with Art. 20 of Regulation (EU) 2019/1020, regardless of whether they have taken action.
enforcementConsequence: Art. 99(4): up to EUR 15 000 000 or 3% of worldwide annual turnover (via Art. 16 provider obligations)

title: Market Surveillance and Control of AI Systems in the Union Market
summary: Establishes the market surveillance framework for AI systems, designating competent authorities, granting access rights to documentation and source code, and specifically providing that for financial institutions, the national authority responsible for financial supervision acts as the market surveillance authority.
body: Art. 74(1) provides that Regulation (EU) 2019/1020 applies to AI systems falling within the scope of this Regulation. For effective enforcement: (a) any reference to an economic operator under Regulation (EU) 2019/1020 shall include all operators identified in Art. 2(1) of this Regulation; (b) any reference to a product under Regulation (EU) 2019/1020 shall include all AI systems falling within the scope of this Regulation. Art. 74(2) requires market surveillance authorities to report annually to the Commission and to the relevant national competition authorities all information identified in the course of market surveillance activities that may be of interest for the application of Union competition law, and to report annually on the application of prohibited practices and measures taken. Art. 74(3) designates the authority appointed for market surveillance under the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I Section A as the market surveillance authority for the purposes of this Regulation for related high-risk AI systems and products. By derogation, Member States may designate another relevant authority under appropriate circumstances, provided coordination with the relevant sectoral market surveillance authorities is ensured. Art. 74(4) provides that the procedures under Articles 79 to 83 shall not apply to AI systems related to products covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I Section A, where those acts already provide for equivalent procedures. Art. 74(5) allows market surveillance authorities to exercise the powers referred to in Art. 14(4)(d) and (j) of Regulation (EU) 2019/1020 remotely where necessary for effective enforcement. Art. 74(6) provides that for high-risk AI systems placed on the market, put into service, or used by financial institutions regulated on the basis of Union financial services law, the national authority designated under those acts for the financial supervision of those institutions shall act as the market surveillance authority for the purposes of this Regulation, insofar as the placing on the market, putting into service, or use of the AI system is directly related to the provision of those financial services. Art. 74(7) allows Member States to designate another relevant authority as market surveillance authority by derogation from paragraph (6) under appropriate circumstances and where coordination is ensured. National market surveillance authorities supervising credit institutions regulated under Directive 2013/36/EU participating in the Single Supervisory Mechanism established by Regulation (EU) No 1024/2013 shall transmit without delay to the European Central Bank any information identified in the course of their market surveillance activities that may be relevant to the ECB's supervisory tasks. Art. 74(8) designates data protection supervisory authorities or other authorities designated under the same conditions as market surveillance authorities for high-risk AI systems used for law enforcement, border management, justice and democracy (Annex III point 1), and for systems listed in Annex III points 6, 7, and 8. Art. 74(9) designates the European Data Protection Supervisor as the market surveillance authority for Union institutions, bodies, offices, and agencies. Art. 74(10) requires Member States to facilitate coordination between market surveillance authorities and other relevant national authorities. Art. 74(11) enables joint activities including joint investigations by market surveillance authorities and the Commission. Art. 74(12) requires providers to grant market surveillance authorities full access to documentation and to training, validation, and testing datasets, including through APIs or other remote access tools. Art. 74(13) grants market surveillance authorities access to the source code of a high-risk AI system upon a reasoned request only where: (a) access is necessary to assess conformity, and (b) testing and auditing procedures based on provider documentation have been exhausted or proved insufficient. Art. 74(14) provides that any information or documentation obtained by market surveillance authorities shall be treated in accordance with the confidentiality obligations laid down in Art. 78.
enforcementConsequence: Framework provision establishing enforcement authorities — no direct fine but enables all enforcement actions

title: Powers of Authorities Protecting Fundamental Rights
summary: Empowers national authorities or public bodies responsible for supervising the protection of fundamental rights (including the right to non-discrimination) to request and access all documentation created or maintained under this Regulation concerning high-risk AI systems listed in Annex III.
body: Art. 77(1) provides that national authorities or public bodies that supervise or enforce the observance of obligations under Union law protecting fundamental rights, including the right to non-discrimination, in relation to the use of high-risk AI systems referred to in Annex III, shall be empowered to request and access any documentation created or maintained under this Regulation in accessible language and format, where access to that documentation is necessary for the effective exercise of their mandates within the limits of their jurisdiction. The relevant authority or public body shall inform the market surveillance authority of the Member State concerned of any such request. Art. 77(2) requires each Member State by 2 November 2024 to identify the authorities or public bodies referred to in paragraph (1) and make them available on a public list. Member States shall notify the list to the Commission and all other Member States and keep the list up to date. Art. 77(3) provides that where the documentation referred to in paragraph (1) does not suffice to ascertain whether an infringement of obligations under Union law protecting fundamental rights has occurred, the authority or public body referred to in paragraph (1) may make a reasoned request to the market surveillance authority to organise a technical test of the high-risk AI system. The market surveillance authority shall organise the test with the close involvement of the requesting authority or public body within a reasonable period following the request. Art. 77(4) provides that any information or documentation obtained by the national authorities or public bodies shall be treated in accordance with the confidentiality obligations laid down in Art. 78.
enforcementConsequence: Framework provision granting fundamental rights authorities access powers — no direct fine but supports enforcement

title: Right to Lodge a Complaint with a Market Surveillance Authority
summary: Grants any natural or legal person the right to lodge complaints with the relevant market surveillance authority if they have reason to believe that the provisions of this Regulation have been infringed.
body: Art. 85 provides that without prejudice to other administrative or judicial remedies, any natural or legal person having grounds to consider that there has been an infringement of the provisions of this Regulation may submit complaints to the relevant market surveillance authority. In accordance with Regulation (EU) 2019/1020, such complaints shall be taken into account for the purpose of conducting market surveillance activities and shall be handled in accordance with the dedicated procedures established by the market surveillance authorities for that purpose.
enforcementConsequence: No direct fine — establishes individual complaint right as enforcement trigger

title: Right to Explanation of Individual Decision-Making
summary: Grants affected persons the right to obtain a clear and meaningful explanation from the deployer regarding the role of the AI system in the decision-making process and the main elements of the decision, where a high-risk AI system (Annex III, except point 2) produces a decision with legal effects or similarly significant effects.
body: Art. 86(1) provides that any person subject to a decision which is taken by the deployer on the basis of the output from a high-risk AI system listed in Annex III, with the exception of systems listed under point 2 thereof, and which produces legal effects concerning that person or similarly significantly affects that person in a way that they consider to have an adverse impact on their health, safety, or fundamental rights, shall have the right to obtain from the deployer clear and meaningful explanations of the role of the AI system in the decision-making procedure and the main elements of the decision taken. Art. 86(2) provides that paragraph (1) shall not apply to the use of AI systems for which exceptions from, or restrictions to, the obligation under that paragraph follow from Union or national law in compliance with Union law. Art. 86(3) provides that this Article shall apply only insofar as the right referred to in paragraph (1) is not otherwise provided for under Union law.
enforcementConsequence: Art. 99(4): up to EUR 15 000 000 or 3% of worldwide annual turnover (via Art. 26 deployer obligations)

title: Reporting of Infringements and Protection of Reporting Persons
summary: Applies Directive (EU) 2019/1937 (Whistleblower Protection Directive) to the reporting of infringements of this Regulation and the protection of persons reporting such infringements.
body: Art. 87 provides that Directive (EU) 2019/1937 shall apply to the reporting of infringements of this Regulation and the protection of persons reporting such infringements.
enforcementConsequence: No direct fine under AI Act — Directive (EU) 2019/1937 provides own enforcement mechanisms

title: Codes of Conduct for Voluntary Application of Specific Requirements
summary: Mandates the AI Office and Member States to encourage and facilitate the drawing up of codes of conduct to foster the voluntary application of some or all Chapter III Section 2 requirements to non-high-risk AI systems, including environmental sustainability, AI literacy, inclusive design, and impact assessment for vulnerable persons.
body: Art. 95(1) requires the AI Office and the Member States to encourage and facilitate the drawing up of codes of conduct, including related governance mechanisms, intended to foster the voluntary application of some or all of the requirements set out in Chapter III Section 2 to AI systems other than high-risk AI systems, taking into account the available technical solutions and industry best practices allowing for the application of such requirements. Art. 95(2) requires the AI Office and the Member States to facilitate the drawing up of codes of conduct regarding the voluntary application of specific requirements to all AI systems, including by deployers, on the basis of clear objectives and key performance indicators to measure the achievement of those objectives, including but not limited to: (a) applicable elements contained in the Union ethics guidelines for trustworthy AI; (b) assessing and minimising the impact of AI systems on environmental sustainability, including as regards energy-efficient programming, and techniques for the efficient design, training, and use of AI; (c) promoting AI literacy, in particular of persons dealing with the development, operation, and use of AI; (d) facilitating an inclusive and diverse design of AI systems, including through the setting up of inclusive and diverse development teams and the promotion of stakeholder participation in that process; (e) assessing and preventing the negative impact of AI systems on vulnerable persons or groups of vulnerable persons, including as regards accessibility for persons with disabilities, as well as on gender equality. Art. 95(3) provides that codes of conduct may be drawn up by individual AI providers or deployers or by organisations representing them or by both, including with the involvement of stakeholders and their representative organisations including civil society organisations and academia. Codes of conduct may cover one or more AI systems taking into account the similarity of the intended purpose of the relevant systems. Art. 95(4) requires the AI Office and the Member States to take into account the specific interests and needs of SMEs, including start-ups, when encouraging and facilitating the drawing up of codes of conduct.
enforcementConsequence: No direct fine — voluntary codes of conduct; non-compliance with voluntary codes has no sanction

title: Penalties
summary: Establishes the three-tier penalty framework: up to EUR 35M/7% for prohibited AI practices (Art. 5), up to EUR 15M/3% for violations of provider/deployer/notified body obligations (Art. 16, 22, 23, 24, 26, 31/33/34, 50), and up to EUR 7.5M/1% for supplying false information. Includes SME cap provisions, detailed aggravating/mitigating factors, and annual reporting obligations.
body: Art. 99(1) requires Member States to lay down rules on penalties and other enforcement measures, which may also include warnings and non-monetary measures, applicable to infringements of this Regulation by operators, taking into account the guidelines issued by the Commission pursuant to Art. 96, and to take all measures necessary for their proper and effective implementation. The penalties provided for shall be effective, proportionate, and dissuasive. They shall take into account the interests of SMEs, including start-ups, and their economic viability. Art. 99(2) requires Member States to notify the Commission of the rules on penalties and other enforcement measures without delay and at the latest by the date of their application, and to notify it without delay of any subsequent amendment. Art. 99(3) provides that non-compliance with the prohibition of AI practices referred to in Art. 5 shall be subject to administrative fines of up to EUR 35 000 000 or, if the offender is an undertaking, up to 7% of its total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher. Art. 99(4) provides that non-compliance with the following provisions relating to operators or notified bodies, other than those laid down in Art. 5, shall be subject to administrative fines of up to EUR 15 000 000 or, if the offender is an undertaking, up to 3% of its total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher: (a) obligations of providers pursuant to Art. 16; (b) obligations of authorised representatives pursuant to Art. 22; (c) obligations of importers pursuant to Art. 23; (d) obligations of distributors pursuant to Art. 24; (e) obligations of deployers pursuant to Art. 26; (f) requirements and obligations of notified bodies pursuant to Art. 31, Art. 33(1), (3) and (4), or Art. 34; (g) transparency obligations for providers and deployers pursuant to Art. 50. Art. 99(5) provides that the supply of incorrect, incomplete, or misleading information to notified bodies or competent national authorities in reply to a request shall be subject to administrative fines of up to EUR 7 500 000 or, if the offender is an undertaking, up to 1% of its total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher. Art. 99(6) provides that in the case of SMEs, including start-ups, each fine referred to in this Article shall be up to the lower of the percentages or amounts referred to in paragraphs (3), (4), and (5). Art. 99(7) provides that when deciding whether to impose a fine and when deciding on the amount, the following shall be taken into account in each individual case: (a) nature, gravity, and duration of the infringement and of its consequences, taking into account the purpose of the AI system and the number of affected persons and the level of damage suffered by them; (b) whether fines have already been applied by other market surveillance authorities for the same infringement; (c) whether fines have already been applied by other authorities for infringements of other Union or national law resulting from the same activity or omission; (d) size, annual turnover, and market share of the operator; (e) any other aggravating or mitigating factors, including financial benefits gained or losses avoided; (f) degree of cooperation with the competent national authorities; (g) degree of responsibility taking into account technical and organisational measures taken; (h) manner in which the infringement became known to the authorities, in particular whether and to what extent the operator notified the infringement; (i) whether the infringement was committed intentionally or negligently; (j) any action taken by the operator to mitigate the damage suffered by affected persons. Art. 99(8) requires each Member State to lay down rules on the extent to which fines may be imposed on public authorities and bodies established in that Member State. Art. 99(9) provides that the rules on fines may be applied so that the fines are imposed by competent national courts or other bodies, provided equivalent effect is ensured. Art. 99(10) requires that the exercise of powers under this Article be subject to appropriate procedural safeguards including effective judicial remedies and due process. Art. 99(11) requires Member States to report annually to the Commission on the fines imposed under this Article and on related litigation or judicial proceedings.
enforcementConsequence: Self-referential: this Article IS the penalty framework (Art. 99(3): 35M/7%, Art. 99(4): 15M/3%, Art. 99(5): 7.5M/1%)

title: Fines for Providers of General-Purpose AI Models
summary: Empowers the Commission to impose fines of up to 3% of worldwide annual turnover or EUR 15 000 000 on providers of general-purpose AI models for intentional or negligent violations of obligations, non-compliance with information requests, failure to comply with measures under Art. 93, or denial of access for evaluation under Art. 92.
body: Art. 101(1) provides that the Commission may impose fines on providers of general-purpose AI models of up to 3% of their total worldwide annual turnover in the preceding financial year or EUR 15 000 000, whichever is higher, where it finds that the provider intentionally or negligently: (a) infringed the relevant provisions of this Regulation; (b) failed to comply with a request for a document or for information pursuant to Art. 91, or supplied incorrect, incomplete, or misleading information; (c) failed to comply with a measure requested under Art. 93; (d) failed to make available to the Commission access to the general-purpose AI model or the general-purpose AI model with systemic risk with a view to conducting an evaluation pursuant to Art. 92. In deciding on the amount of the fine or periodic penalty payment, due regard shall be given to the nature, gravity, and duration of the infringement, as well as the principles of proportionality and appropriateness. The Commission shall also take into account commitments made in accordance with Art. 93(3) or provided for in the relevant codes of practice pursuant to Art. 56. Art. 101(2) requires the Commission to communicate its preliminary assessment to the provider of the general-purpose AI model before adopting a decision under paragraph (1) and give the provider the opportunity to be heard. Art. 101(3) requires the fines imposed under this Article to be effective, proportionate, and dissuasive. Art. 101(4) provides that information about fines imposed under this Article shall be communicated to the AI Board as appropriate. Art. 101(5) provides that the Court of Justice of the European Union shall have unlimited jurisdiction to review the Commission's decisions setting a fine under this Article, and may annul, reduce, or increase the fine imposed. Art. 101(6) requires the Commission to adopt implementing acts laying down detailed arrangements and procedural safeguards for proceedings in view of the possible adoption of decisions pursuant to paragraph (1), to be adopted in accordance with the examination procedure referred to in Art. 98(2).
enforcementConsequence: Direct: Commission may impose up to EUR 15 000 000 or 3% of worldwide annual turnover on GPAI model providers

title: Measures for SMEs Including Start-ups
summary: Requires Member States to support SMEs and start-ups with prioritised sandbox access, training, communication channels, and standardisation participation. The AI Office must provide templates, a central information platform, awareness campaigns, and promote best practices in AI-related procurement.
body: Art. 62(1) requires Member States to undertake the following measures: (a) grant SMEs, including start-ups, having their registered office or a branch in the Union, priority access to AI regulatory sandboxes, to the extent that they fulfil the eligibility conditions and selection criteria; priority access shall not preclude other SMEs and start-ups from accessing the sandbox provided they also meet eligibility conditions; (b) organise specific awareness-raising and training activities on the application of this Regulation tailored to the needs of SMEs, including start-ups, deployers, and where appropriate, local public authorities; (c) utilise existing dedicated channels and where appropriate establish new ones for communication with SMEs, including start-ups, deployers, other innovators, and where appropriate, local public authorities to provide advice and respond to queries about the implementation of this Regulation, including on participation in AI regulatory sandboxes; (d) facilitate the participation of SMEs and other relevant stakeholders in the standardisation development process. Art. 62(2) requires that, when setting conformity assessment fees under Art. 43, the specific interests and needs of SMEs, including start-ups, shall be taken into account by reducing those fees proportionately to the size of the undertaking, its market size, and other relevant indicators. Art. 62(3) requires the AI Office to undertake the following actions: (a) provide standardised templates for areas covered by this Regulation, as specified by the AI Board in its request; (b) develop and maintain a single information platform providing easy-to-use information in relation to this Regulation for all operators across the Union; (c) organise appropriate communication campaigns to raise awareness about obligations arising from this Regulation; (d) evaluate and promote the convergence of best practices in public procurement procedures in relation to AI systems.
financialSectorGuidance: Financial institutions deploying high-risk AI systems (e.g. credit scoring under Anhang III Nr. 5(b)) should leverage the proportionate conformity assessment fees for SME-sized fintechs. BaFin-supervised entities should use the AI Office's central information platform and standardised templates for their AI Act compliance documentation. The sandbox priority access provision is particularly relevant for RegTech/FinTech start-ups developing AI-based compliance solutions.
enforcementConsequence: Member State obligation — no direct fine for providers, but failure to implement may lead to Commission infringement proceedings against the Member State

title: Transitional Provisions for Existing AI Systems and GPAI Models
summary: Establishes transitional periods for AI systems and GPAI models already on the market. IT large-scale systems under Annex X must comply by 31 December 2030. High-risk systems placed on the market before 2 August 2026 are only covered if significantly modified. GPAI models placed on the market before 2 August 2025 must comply by 2 August 2027.
body: Art. 111(1) provides that, without prejudice to the application of Art. 5 in accordance with Art. 113(3)(a), AI systems which are components of large-scale IT systems established by the legislative acts listed in Annex X and which have been placed on the market or put into service before 2 August 2027, shall be brought into compliance with this Regulation by 31 December 2030. The requirements laid down in this Regulation shall be taken into account in the evaluation of each large-scale IT system established by the legislative acts listed in Annex X, where that evaluation is carried out as provided for in those respective acts and upon replacement or amendment of those legal acts. Art. 111(2) provides that, without prejudice to the application of Art. 5 in accordance with Art. 113(3)(a), this Regulation shall apply to operators of high-risk AI systems — other than those referred to in paragraph 1 — that have been placed on the market or put into service before 2 August 2026, only if, from that date, those systems are subject to significant changes in their design. In any event, providers and deployers of high-risk AI systems intended to be used by public authorities shall take the necessary steps to comply with the requirements and obligations of this Regulation by 2 August 2030. Art. 111(3) provides that providers of general-purpose AI models that have been placed on the market before 2 August 2025 shall take the necessary steps to comply with the obligations laid down in this Regulation by 2 August 2027.
financialSectorGuidance: Critical for legacy AI systems in banking and insurance. Credit scoring models, algorithmic trading systems, or insurance risk models placed on the market before 2 August 2026 are only affected if their design is significantly changed after that date. Financial institutions used by public authorities (e.g. KfW, Landesbanken) must comply by 2 August 2030 regardless. GPAI models used in financial services (e.g. foundation models for document processing) that were deployed before August 2025 have until August 2027 to comply. Institutions should conduct an inventory of all AI systems with deployment dates to determine applicable transition timelines.
enforcementConsequence: Failure to comply within transitional periods triggers full enforcement regime including fines under Art. 99

title: Entry into Force and Application Dates
summary: Defines the phased application timeline of the AI Act. The Regulation entered into force on the 20th day after publication and applies generally from 2 August 2026. Prohibited practices (Chapter I+II) apply from 2 February 2025. GPAI rules, governance, and penalties (Chapter III Section 4, V, VII, XII, Art. 78) apply from 2 August 2025 (except Art. 101). Art. 6(1) high-risk classification applies from 2 August 2027.
body: Art. 113 states that this Regulation shall enter into force on the twentieth day following that of its publication in the Official Journal of the European Union. It shall apply from 2 August 2026. However: (a) Chapters I and II shall apply from 2 February 2025; (b) Chapter III Section 4, Chapter V, Chapter VII and Chapter XII and Article 78 shall apply from 2 August 2025, with the exception of Article 101; (c) Article 6(1) and the corresponding obligations under this Regulation shall apply from 2 August 2027. This Regulation shall be binding in its entirety and directly applicable in all Member States. Done at Brussels, 13 June 2024.
financialSectorGuidance: Key compliance milestones for financial institutions: (1) Since 2 February 2025, the prohibited AI practices under Art. 5 already apply — social scoring and manipulative AI are banned. (2) Since 2 August 2025, GPAI obligations (Chapter V) and governance provisions (Chapter VII) apply. (3) From 2 August 2026, the full Regulation applies including high-risk requirements for credit scoring (Anhang III Nr. 5(b)) and insurance pricing (Anhang III Nr. 5(c)). (4) From 2 August 2027, Art. 6(1) classification for AI embedded in products under Annex I harmonisation legislation applies. Financial institutions should already have completed their Art. 5 compliance assessment and should now focus on high-risk system documentation for the August 2026 deadline.
enforcementConsequence: Provisions become enforceable at their respective application dates — non-compliance triggers sanctions under Art. 99

title: Annex I — Union Harmonisation Legislation
summary: Lists EU harmonisation legislation relevant to Art. 6(1) high-risk classification. Section A covers New Legislative Framework legislation (12 items: machinery, toys, lifts, pressure equipment, medical devices, etc.). Section B covers other harmonisation legislation (8 items: civil aviation, vehicles, ships, railways).
body: Anhang I lists the Union harmonisation legislation referred to in Art. 6(1) for high-risk classification. Section A — Union harmonisation legislation based on the New Legislative Framework: (1) Directive 2006/42/EC on machinery; (2) Directive 2009/48/EC on toy safety; (3) Directive 2013/53/EU on recreational craft; (4) Directive 2014/33/EU on lifts; (5) Directive 2014/34/EU on equipment for use in potentially explosive atmospheres; (6) Directive 2014/53/EU on radio equipment; (7) Directive 2014/68/EU on pressure equipment; (8) Regulation (EU) 2016/424 on cableway installations; (9) Regulation (EU) 2016/425 on personal protective equipment; (10) Regulation (EU) 2016/426 on appliances burning gaseous fuels; (11) Regulation (EU) 2017/745 on medical devices; (12) Regulation (EU) 2017/746 on in vitro diagnostic medical devices. Section B — Other Union harmonisation legislation: (13) Regulation (EC) No 300/2008 on civil aviation security; (14) Regulation (EU) No 168/2013 on two- or three-wheel vehicles and quadricycles; (15) Regulation (EU) No 167/2013 on agricultural and forestry vehicles; (16) Directive 2014/90/EU on marine equipment; (17) Directive (EU) 2016/797 on rail interoperability; (18) Regulation (EU) 2018/858 on motor vehicles; (19) Regulation (EU) 2019/2144 on type-approval of motor vehicles (general safety); (20) Regulation (EU) 2018/1139 on civil aviation (insofar as unmanned aircraft and their components are concerned).
financialSectorGuidance: Not directly applicable to financial services. Annex I covers product safety legislation (machinery, medical devices, vehicles). Financial sector AI systems are classified as high-risk under Art. 6(2) via Anhang III, not via Art. 6(1)/Anhang I. However, financial institutions providing AI-based components integrated into products listed here (e.g. AI for autonomous vehicle financing risk models) should be aware of the dual classification pathway.
enforcementConsequence: AI systems that are safety components of products under these directives/regulations are automatically high-risk under Art. 6(1)

title: Annex II — Criminal Offences for Biometric Identification
summary: Lists the criminal offences under Art. 5(1)(h)(iii) for which real-time remote biometric identification may be permitted. Includes terrorism, trafficking in human beings, child sexual exploitation, drug trafficking, arms trafficking, murder, organ trafficking, nuclear materials trafficking, kidnapping, ICC crimes, hijacking, rape, environmental crime, armed robbery, sabotage, and participation in a criminal organisation involved in these offences.
body: Anhang II lists criminal offences referred to in Art. 5(1) subparagraph 1 point (h)(iii): terrorism; trafficking in human beings; sexual exploitation of children and child pornography; illicit trafficking in narcotic drugs or psychotropic substances; illicit trafficking in weapons, munitions, or explosives; murder, grievous bodily harm; illicit trafficking in human organs or tissue; illicit trafficking in nuclear or radioactive materials; kidnapping, unlawful restraint, or hostage-taking; crimes within the jurisdiction of the International Criminal Court; hijacking of aircraft or ships; rape; environmental crime; organised or armed robbery; sabotage; participation in a criminal organisation that is involved in one or more of the offences listed above.
financialSectorGuidance: Not directly applicable to financial services. This annex concerns law enforcement use of real-time biometric identification. However, financial institutions should note that several listed offences (terrorism, drug trafficking, arms trafficking) overlap with AML/CFT obligations under the Anti-Money Laundering Directive. AI systems used for AML transaction monitoring are not subject to this annex but may interact with law enforcement systems that are.
enforcementConsequence: Use of real-time biometric identification outside these listed offences is prohibited under Art. 5 — fines up to EUR 35 million or 7% of global turnover

title: Annex III — High-Risk AI Systems
summary: Defines the 8 areas of high-risk AI systems under Art. 6(2): (1) biometrics, (2) critical infrastructure, (3) education, (4) employment, (5) essential services including credit scoring and insurance pricing, (6) law enforcement, (7) migration/asylum/border control, (8) justice and democratic processes.
body: Anhang III lists high-risk AI systems pursuant to Art. 6(2). Area 1 — Biometrics (where permitted by EU/national law): (a) remote biometric identification systems (excluding verification-only systems); (b) biometric categorisation by sensitive or protected attributes; (c) emotion recognition systems. Area 2 — Critical infrastructure: AI systems intended as safety components in the management and operation of critical digital infrastructure, road traffic, or water, gas, heating, and electricity supply. Area 3 — Education and vocational training: (a) access/admission determination or assignment to educational institutions; (b) evaluation of learning outcomes including steering of learning processes; (c) assessment of appropriate education level; (d) monitoring and detection of prohibited behaviour during examinations. Area 4 — Employment, workers management, and access to self-employment: (a) recruitment or selection of persons, including targeted job advertisements, screening/filtering applications, and evaluating candidates; (b) decisions affecting terms of work relationships, promotions, terminations, task allocation based on individual behaviour or personal traits, and monitoring/evaluating performance. Area 5 — Access to and enjoyment of essential private and public services and benefits: (a) AI used by/for public authorities to assess eligibility for public assistance and services; (b) creditworthiness assessment and credit scoring of natural persons (except fraud detection); (c) risk assessment and pricing for natural persons in life and health insurance; (d) evaluation and classification of emergency calls and dispatching/prioritisation of emergency services including patient triage. Area 6 — Law enforcement (where permitted): (a) individual risk assessment of becoming a victim; (b) polygraphs and similar tools; (c) reliability assessment of evidence; (d) risk assessment of committing/reoffending; (e) profiling in detection/investigation/prosecution. Area 7 — Migration, asylum, and border control (where permitted): (a) polygraphs and similar; (b) risk assessment by persons at border; (c) examination of asylum/visa applications; (d) detection/recognition/identification of persons. Area 8 — Administration of justice and democratic processes: (a) AI used by/for judicial authorities to assist in researching and interpreting facts and law; (b) AI to influence election/referendum outcomes or voting behaviour (excluding campaign logistics tools).
financialSectorGuidance: Directly applicable to financial institutions via Area 5: (b) Credit scoring and creditworthiness assessment of natural persons is high-risk (exception: fraud detection AI). This covers all AI-based Schufa-style scoring, loan approval models, and automated creditworthiness tools. (c) Risk assessment and pricing for natural persons in life and health insurance is high-risk. This covers actuarial AI models, risk-based premium calculation, and underwriting automation. Financial institutions using these AI systems must comply with all high-risk obligations under Chapter III Section 2 (Art. 8–15), including risk management (Art. 9), data governance (Art. 10), transparency (Art. 13), and human oversight (Art. 14).
enforcementConsequence: AI systems falling under Annex III are subject to full high-risk obligations — non-compliance fines up to EUR 15 million or 3% of global turnover under Art. 99

title: Annex IV — Technical Documentation
summary: Specifies the minimum content of technical documentation under Art. 11(1) for high-risk AI systems. Covers 9 areas: general system description, detailed development process, monitoring/operation/control information, performance metrics justification, risk management description, lifecycle changes, applied standards, EU declaration of conformity, and post-market monitoring system.
body: Anhang IV requires the technical documentation referred to in Art. 11(1) to contain at minimum the following information, insofar as relevant: (1) General description of the AI system, including: (a) intended purpose, provider name, and system version with relation to previous versions; (b) interaction with hardware or software not part of the system; (c) software/firmware versions and update requirements; (d) description of all forms of market placement (embedded software, download, API); (e) description of hardware on which the system operates; (f) photographs/illustrations showing external features and internal layout for product-embedded AI; (g) basic description of user interface provided to deployers; (h) instructions for use and basic description of the user interface. (2) Detailed description of system elements and development process, including: (a) methods and steps for development, including use of pre-trained third-party systems and how they were used, integrated, or modified; (b) design specifications including general logic and algorithms, key design decisions with rationale and assumptions (including regarding persons/groups the system applies to), main classification choices, optimisation objectives, parameter significance, expected output quality, and trade-off decisions regarding Chapter III Section 2 requirements; (c) system architecture showing how software components build on each other and integrate, and computational resources used for development, training, testing, and validation; (d) data requirements via datasheets describing training methods/techniques and datasets, including general description, provenance, scope, main characteristics, data procurement and selection, labelling procedures, and data cleaning methods; (e) assessment of human oversight measures under Art. 14, with assessment of technical measures for facilitating output interpretation per Art. 13(3)(d); (f) description of predetermined changes and performance with information on technical solutions ensuring continued compliance with Chapter III Section 2; (g) validation and testing procedures with information on data used, main characteristics, parameters for measuring accuracy, robustness, other requirements, and potentially discriminatory impacts, test protocols and dated/signed test reports; (h) cybersecurity measures taken. (3) Detailed information on monitoring, functioning, and control of the system: capabilities and performance limitations, accuracy levels for specific persons/groups, expected overall accuracy, foreseeable unintended outcomes and risk sources, human oversight measures including technical measures facilitating output interpretation, input data specifications where applicable. (4) Justification of the appropriateness of performance metrics. (5) Detailed description of the risk management system under Art. 9. (6) Description of relevant changes made during the lifecycle. (7) List of applied harmonised standards or detailed description of alternative solutions, with list of other relevant standards and technical specifications. (8) Copy of the EU declaration of conformity under Art. 47. (9) Detailed description of the post-market performance evaluation system under Art. 72, including the post-market monitoring plan under Art. 72(3).
financialSectorGuidance: Essential for financial institutions developing or deploying high-risk AI systems. Credit scoring and insurance pricing models must have comprehensive technical documentation covering: model architecture and algorithm design rationale (2b), training data provenance and bias detection methods (2d) — critical for fair lending compliance, validation/testing procedures including discriminatory impact assessment (2g) — aligns with EBA Guidelines on loan origination, cybersecurity measures (2h) — overlaps with DORA requirements, and human oversight measures (2e/3) — aligns with MaRisk AT 4.3.1 on model risk management. Financial supervisors (BaFin, ECB) may request access to this documentation during inspections.
enforcementConsequence: Insufficient technical documentation is a violation of Art. 11 — fines up to EUR 15 million or 3% of global turnover under Art. 99

title: Annex V — EU Declaration of Conformity
summary: Specifies the 8 mandatory elements of the EU declaration of conformity under Art. 47: system name/identification, provider details, provider responsibility statement, conformity assurance, data protection compliance statement, harmonised standards references, notified body details if applicable, and place/date/signatory details.
body: Anhang V requires the EU declaration of conformity referred to in Art. 47 to contain all of the following information: (1) Name and type of the AI system and any additional unambiguous reference allowing identification and traceability of the AI system. (2) Name and address of the provider and, where applicable, of their authorised representative. (3) Statement that the provider bears sole responsibility for the issuance of the EU declaration of conformity pursuant to Art. 47. (4) Assurance that the AI system in question conforms to this Regulation and, where applicable, to any other relevant Union legislation providing for the issuance of the EU declaration of conformity pursuant to Art. 47. (5) Where an AI system involves the processing of personal data, a statement that the AI system complies with Regulations (EU) 2016/679 and (EU) 2018/1725 and Directive (EU) 2016/680. (6) References to any relevant harmonised standards or other common specifications used for which conformity is declared. (7) Where applicable, name and identification number of the notified body, description of the conformity assessment procedure performed, and identification number of the certificate issued. (8) Place and date of issue of the declaration, name and function of the signatory, indication of on whose behalf they signed, and a signature.
financialSectorGuidance: Financial institutions acting as providers of high-risk AI systems (e.g. proprietary credit scoring models offered to other institutions) must issue this declaration before placing the system on the market. Element (5) on GDPR/data protection compliance is particularly relevant given the sensitivity of financial data processing. The declaration must be kept up to date and made available to supervisory authorities (BaFin, ECB-SSM) on request. Deployer-only institutions do not issue this declaration themselves but should verify that their AI system providers have issued one.
enforcementConsequence: Failure to draw up or keep available the EU declaration of conformity is a violation of Art. 47 — fines up to EUR 15 million or 3% of global turnover

title: Annex VI — Conformity Assessment Based on Internal Control
summary: Defines the internal control conformity assessment procedure in 4 steps: (1) scope definition referring to steps 2–4, (2) verification that the QMS meets Art. 17 requirements, (3) examination of technical documentation against Chapter III Section 2 requirements, (4) verification that the design/development process and post-market monitoring comply with the technical documentation.
body: Anhang VI defines the conformity assessment procedure based on internal control: (1) The conformity assessment procedure based on internal control is the conformity assessment procedure pursuant to points 2, 3, and 4. (2) The provider shall verify that the existing quality management system complies with the requirements of Art. 17. (3) The provider shall examine the information contained in the technical documentation to assess whether the AI system complies with the relevant essential requirements laid down in Chapter III Section 2. (4) The provider shall also verify that the design and development process of the AI system and its post-market monitoring referred to in Art. 72 are consistent with the technical documentation.
financialSectorGuidance: This is the default conformity assessment path for most financial sector high-risk AI systems. Credit scoring models and insurance pricing AI can use internal control (Anhang VI) rather than third-party assessment (Anhang VII), unless they fall under Annex I product legislation. Financial institutions should integrate these 4 verification steps into their existing model validation framework (MaRisk AT 4.3.1). The QMS verification (step 2) aligns with existing internal audit requirements under CRD/CRR. The technical documentation examination (step 3) should be documented as part of the model risk management process.
enforcementConsequence: Failure to conduct proper conformity assessment is a violation of Art. 43 — fines up to EUR 15 million or 3% of global turnover

title: Annex VII — Conformity Assessment Based on QMS and Technical Documentation Review
summary: Defines the third-party conformity assessment procedure involving a notified body.
