Covers 5 areas: (1) introduction, (2) overview of QMS approval and technical documentation review, (3) QMS assessment including application requirements, evaluation, ongoing maintenance, and change management, (4) technical documentation control including examination, testing, access to training data, and Union certificate issuance, (5) ongoing surveillance of the approved QMS including regular audits.
body: Anhang VII defines the conformity procedure based on quality management system assessment and technical documentation assessment. (1) Introduction: This procedure corresponds to the conformity assessment pursuant to points 2 to 5. (2) Overview: The approved QMS for the design, development, and testing of AI systems under Art. 17 is examined under point 3 and subject to surveillance under point 5. The technical documentation of the AI system is examined under point 4. (3) Quality management system — (3.1) The provider's application must contain: (a) name and address; (b) list of AI systems covered by the same QMS; (c) technical documentation for each AI system; (d) QMS documentation covering all aspects in Art. 17; (e) description of procedures ensuring the QMS remains adequate and effective; (f) written declaration that the same application has not been lodged with any other notified body. (3.2) The QMS is assessed by the notified body to determine whether it meets Art. 17 requirements; the decision is communicated with a reasoned assessment. (3.3) The approved QMS shall continue to be applied and maintained by the provider. (3.4) The provider shall inform the notified body of any intended change to the approved QMS or the list of covered AI systems; the notified body examines changes and decides whether re-assessment is needed. (4) Control of technical documentation — (4.1) Provider applies for technical documentation assessment with a notified body of their choice. (4.2) Application contains: provider details, written declaration of no duplicate application, and technical documentation per Anhang IV. (4.3) The notified body examines the technical documentation; where relevant and limited to what is necessary, the notified body has full access to training, validation, and test datasets, including through API or other appropriate technical means enabling remote access. (4.4) The notified body may require further evidence or tests; where dissatisfied with provider testing, it may conduct its own tests. (4.5) Where necessary, access to training models and trained models including relevant parameters is granted, subject to IP and trade secret protections. (4.6) Decision is communicated with a reasoned assessment; where compliant, a Union technical documentation assessment certificate is issued containing provider details, examination results, validity conditions, and AI system identification data. (4.7) Any change affecting compliance or intended purpose requires assessment by the issuing notified body; the notified body decides whether a new conformity assessment under Art. 43(4) is required or a supplement to the certificate suffices. (5) Surveillance of the approved QMS — (5.1) Surveillance ensures the provider properly meets the approved QMS conditions. (5.2) The provider grants the notified body access to design, development, and testing premises and provides all necessary information. (5.3) The notified body carries out periodic audits and may subject certified AI systems to additional testing.
financialSectorGuidance: This third-party assessment path applies when financial sector AI systems also fall under Annex I product legislation (rare for pure financial services). More commonly, financial institutions may voluntarily choose this path for reputational assurance. The notified body's access to training data (4.3) and trained models (4.5) has implications for proprietary model protection — trade secret safeguards apply but institutions should prepare for external scrutiny. The ongoing surveillance requirement (5) creates a continuous compliance obligation beyond initial certification.
enforcementConsequence: Failure to conduct proper third-party conformity assessment where required is a violation of Art. 43 — fines up to EUR 15 million or 3% of global turnover

title: Annex VIII — Registration Information for High-Risk AI Systems
summary: Specifies the information required for registering high-risk AI systems in the EU database under Art. 49. Three sections: Section A (13 items for providers under Art. 49(1)), Section B (9 items for providers of non-high-risk systems under Art. 49(2)), and Section C (5 items for deployers of high-risk systems under Art. 49(3)), including fundamental rights impact assessment summary.
body: Anhang VIII specifies the information to be provided when registering high-risk AI systems pursuant to Art. 49. Section A — Information by providers under Art. 49(1): (1) provider name, address, contact details; (2) name, address, contact details of submitting person if different; (3) authorised representative details where applicable; (4) trade name and additional unambiguous references for identification and traceability; (5) description of intended purpose and supported components/functions; (6) basic and concise description of information used (data, inputs) and operating logic; (7) status of the AI system (on the market/in service; no longer on the market/in service; recalled); (8) type, number, and expiry date of certificate issued by notified body and notified body name/identification; (9) scanned copy of certificate where applicable; (10) all Member States where the system has been placed on the market, put into service, or made available; (11) copy of the EU declaration of conformity under Art. 47; (12) electronic instructions for use (not applicable to law enforcement or migration/border systems under Anhang III Nos. 1, 6, 7); (13) URL for additional information (optional). Section B — Information by providers under Art. 49(2): (1) provider details; (2) submitting person details if different; (3) authorised representative details; (4) trade name and identification; (5) description of intended purpose; (6) condition(s) under Art. 6(3) why the system is not classified as high-risk; (7) brief summary of reasons for non-high-risk classification; (8) system status; (9) all Member States where made available. Section C — Information by deployers under Art. 49(3): (1) deployer name, address, contact details; (2) name, address, contact details of information submitter; (3) URL of the provider's EU database entry; (4) summary of fundamental rights impact assessment results under Art. 27; (5) where applicable, summary of data protection impact assessment under Art. 35 GDPR or Art. 27 of Directive (EU) 2016/680, per Art. 26(8).
financialSectorGuidance: Financial institutions deploying high-risk AI systems (credit scoring, insurance pricing) must register under Section C and provide: (4) a summary of their fundamental rights impact assessment — this is a new obligation without direct precedent in financial regulation; and (5) a DPIA summary where applicable, aligning with existing GDPR obligations. Providers of credit scoring AI must register under Section A with full details including the EU declaration of conformity. The registration creates a public record — financial institutions should coordinate with their legal/compliance teams on what information becomes publicly accessible vs. confidential.
enforcementConsequence: Failure to register or provide required information is a violation of Art. 49 — fines up to EUR 15 million or 3% of global turnover

title: Annex XI — Technical Documentation for GPAI Model Providers
summary: Specifies technical documentation requirements for general-purpose AI (GPAI) model providers under Art. 53(1)(a). Section 1 covers all GPAI providers (general description, development process including training data, compute resources, energy consumption). Section 2 adds requirements for systemic risk GPAI models (evaluation strategies, red teaming, system architecture).
body: Anhang XI requires the technical documentation referred to in Art. 53(1)(a) to contain at minimum the following information, proportionate to the size and risk profile of the model. Section 1 — Information to be provided by all providers of GPAI models: (1) General description including: (a) tasks the model is intended to perform and types of AI systems it may be integrated into; (b) acceptable use policies; (c) date of release and distribution methods; (d) architecture and number of parameters; (e) modality (e.g. text, image) and format of inputs and outputs; (f) licence. (2) Detailed description of model elements and development process, including: (a) technical means (e.g. instructions for use, infrastructure, tools) required for integrating the GPAI model into AI systems; (b) design specifications and training process including training methods and techniques, key design decisions with rationale and assumptions, optimisation objectives and parameter significance where applicable; (c) information on training, testing, and validation data including type, provenance, preparation methods (e.g. cleaning, filtering), number of data points, scope, main characteristics, data procurement and selection methods, measures to detect unsuitable data sources, and methods to detect identifiable biases where applicable; (d) computational resources used for training (e.g. number of floating-point operations), training time, and other relevant training details; (e) known or estimated energy consumption of the model (may be based on computational resource information where consumption is unknown). Section 2 — Additional information for providers of GPAI models with systemic risk: (1) Detailed description of evaluation strategies including results, based on publicly available evaluation protocols and tools or other evaluation methodologies, covering evaluation criteria, metrics, and methodology for identifying limitations. (2) Where applicable, detailed description of measures taken to conduct internal and/or external adversarial testing (e.g. red teaming), model adaptations including alignment and fine-tuning. (3) Where applicable, detailed description of system architecture showing how software components build on each other or feed into each other and integrate into the overall processing.
financialSectorGuidance: Relevant for financial institutions that develop or fine-tune their own GPAI models (e.g. large language models for document analysis, customer service automation). If a financial institution places a GPAI model on the market (e.g. a specialized financial LLM), it must produce this documentation. More commonly, financial institutions are downstream deployers of third-party GPAI models — in this case, they should request Anhang XI documentation from their GPAI provider (e.g. OpenAI, Anthropic, Google) to fulfil their own due diligence obligations. Energy consumption disclosure (1.2.e) may also be relevant for ESG reporting.
enforcementConsequence: Non-compliance with GPAI documentation obligations — fines up to EUR 15 million or 3% of global turnover under Art. 101

title: Annex XII — Transparency Information for Downstream GPAI Integrators
summary: Specifies the transparency information GPAI model providers must make available to downstream providers integrating the model into their AI systems, under Art. 53(1)(b). Covers general model description (tasks, usage policies, release date, architecture, modalities, licence) and development process description (integration tools, input/output formats and limits, training data information).
body: Anhang XII requires the information referred to in Art. 53(1)(b) to contain at minimum the following: (1) General description of the GPAI model including: (a) the tasks the model is intended to perform and the type and nature of AI systems into which it can be integrated; (b) applicable acceptable use policies; (c) date of release and distribution methods; (d) where applicable, how the model interacts with or can be used to interact with hardware or software that is not part of the model itself; (e) where applicable, versions of relevant software related to the use of the GPAI model; (f) architecture and number of parameters; (g) modality (e.g. text, image) and format of inputs and outputs; (h) licence for the model. (2) Description of model elements and development process, including: (a) technical means (e.g. instructions for use, infrastructure, tools) required for integrating the GPAI model into AI systems; (b) modality (e.g. text, image etc.) and format of inputs and outputs and their maximum size (e.g. context window length etc.); (c) where applicable, information on training, testing, and validation data including type, provenance, and preparation methods.
financialSectorGuidance: Directly relevant for financial institutions integrating third-party GPAI models into their AI systems (e.g. using GPT-4 or Claude for automated document analysis, customer service, or regulatory reporting). Financial institutions should demand this documentation from their GPAI providers before integration, as it forms the basis for their own compliance obligations under the AI Act. The context window limitations (2b) and training data information (2c) are essential for assessing model suitability for financial use cases. This transparency information should be incorporated into the institution's third-party risk management framework (MaRisk AT 9).
enforcementConsequence: Non-compliance with GPAI transparency obligations — fines up to EUR 15 million or 3% of global turnover under Art. 101

title: Annex XIII — Criteria for Systemic Risk GPAI Models
summary: Defines the criteria the Commission uses to determine whether a GPAI model has capabilities or impact equivalent to those triggering systemic risk classification under Art. 51(1)(a). Considers 7 factors: number of parameters, dataset quality/size, training compute (FLOPs), input/output modalities and state-of-the-art thresholds, benchmark evaluations, internal market impact (threshold: 10,000 registered business users in the EU), and number of registered end users.
body: Anhang XIII establishes the criteria for designating GPAI models with systemic risk pursuant to Art. 51. To determine whether a GPAI model has capabilities or an impact equivalent to those set out in Art. 51(1)(a), the Commission shall consider the following criteria: (a) the number of parameters of the model; (b) the quality or size of the dataset, for example measured through tokens; (c) the amount of computation used for training the model, measured in floating-point operations or indicated by a combination of other variables such as estimated training cost, estimated time for training, or estimated energy consumption for training; (d) the input and output modalities of the model, such as text-to-text (large language models), text-to-image, multi-modality, state-of-the-art thresholds for determining high-impact capabilities for each modality, and the specific type of inputs and outputs (e.g. biological sequences); (e) the benchmarks and evaluations of capabilities of the model, including considering the number of tasks without additional training, adaptability to learn new distinct tasks, the degree of autonomy and scalability, and the tools it has access to; (f) whether it has a high impact on the internal market due to its reach — this is presumed when it has been made available to at least 10,000 registered business users established in the Union; (g) the number of registered end users.
financialSectorGuidance: Relevant for financial institutions assessing whether GPAI models they use or develop may trigger systemic risk classification. The 10,000 business user threshold (criterion f) is particularly relevant for widely-deployed financial AI platforms (e.g. Bloomberg Terminal AI, Refinitiv AI). Financial institutions developing proprietary large-scale models should monitor their parameter count and compute usage against Art. 51 thresholds (currently set at 10^25 FLOPs). Models classified as systemic risk face additional obligations including adversarial testing, incident reporting, and cybersecurity measures — aligning with DORA requirements for ICT risk management in financial services.
enforcementConsequence: GPAI models meeting these criteria are subject to additional obligations under Art. 55 — non-compliance fines up to EUR 15 million or 3% of global turnover

title: Exemption from Conformity Assessment Procedure
summary: Allows market surveillance authorities to exceptionally authorise the placing on the market or putting into service of specific high-risk AI systems without prior conformity assessment, on grounds of public security, protection of life/health, environmental protection, or protection of key industrial/infrastructure assets. Law enforcement and civil protection authorities may deploy in urgent cases with post-hoc authorisation. Products under Annex I Section A legislation follow sectoral exemptions only.
body: Art. 46(1) provides that, by way of derogation from Art. 43 and upon a duly justified request, any market surveillance authority may authorise the placing on the market or putting into service of specific high-risk AI systems within the territory of the Member State concerned, for exceptional reasons of public security or the protection of life and health of persons, environmental protection, or the protection of key industrial and infrastructure assets. That authorisation shall be for a limited period while the necessary conformity assessment procedures are being carried out, taking into account the exceptional reasons justifying the derogation. The completion of those procedures shall be undertaken without undue delay. Art. 46(2) provides that in a duly justified situation of urgency for exceptional reasons of public security or in case of specific, substantial, and imminent threat to the life or physical safety of natural persons, law enforcement authorities or civil protection authorities may put a specific high-risk AI system into service without the authorisation referred to in paragraph 1, provided that such authorisation is requested during or after the use without undue delay. If the authorisation referred to in paragraph 1 is refused, the use of the high-risk AI system shall be stopped with immediate effect and all results and outputs of that use shall be immediately discarded. Art. 46(3) provides that the authorisation referred to in paragraph 1 shall only be issued if the market surveillance authority concludes that the high-risk AI system complies with the requirements of Section 2. The market surveillance authority shall inform the Commission and the other Member States of any authorisation issued pursuant to paragraphs 1 and 2. That obligation shall not cover sensitive operational data in relation to the activities of law enforcement authorities. Art. 46(4) provides that where, within 15 calendar days of receipt of the information referred to in paragraph 3, no objection has been raised by either a Member State or the Commission against an authorisation issued by a market surveillance authority of a Member State in accordance with paragraph 1, that authorisation shall be deemed justified. Art. 46(5) provides that where, within 15 calendar days of receipt of the notification referred to in paragraph 3, objections are raised by a Member State against an authorisation issued by a market surveillance authority of another Member State, or where the Commission considers the authorisation to be contrary to Union law or the conclusion of the Member States regarding the conformity of the system referred to in paragraph 3 to be unfounded, the Commission shall without delay enter into consultations with the relevant Member State. The operators concerned shall be consulted and have the opportunity to present their views. Having regard thereto, the Commission shall decide whether the authorisation is justified. The Commission shall address its decision to the Member State concerned and to the relevant operators. Art. 46(6) provides that if the authorisation is considered unjustified by the Commission, it shall be withdrawn by the market surveillance authority of the Member State concerned. Art. 46(7) provides that for high-risk AI systems related to products covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I Section A, only the derogations from the conformity assessment established in that Union harmonisation legislation shall apply.
financialSectorGuidance: Limited direct applicability for financial institutions. This exemption targets public security and emergency scenarios (law enforcement, civil protection). Financial supervisory authorities (BaFin, ECB-SSM) acting as market surveillance authorities under Art. 74 could theoretically invoke this provision for AI systems critical to financial stability (e.g. systemic risk monitoring tools), but the threshold is very high and requires exceptional circumstances. Financial institutions cannot self-invoke this exemption — it requires explicit market surveillance authority approval.
enforcementConsequence: No direct fine provision — procedural exemption provision; misuse may be sanctionable via general market surveillance enforcement

title: Codes of Practice for GPAI
summary: Requires the AI Office to encourage and facilitate the development of codes of practice at Union level for GPAI obligations under Art. 53 and 55. Codes must cover information currency, training content summaries, systemic risk identification and management. Involves stakeholder participation including civil society, industry, and academia. Includes KPI-based monitoring, Commission approval by implementing act, and a deadline of 2 May 2025 for initial codes. If codes are inadequate by 2 August 2025, the Commission may adopt implementing acts establishing common rules.
body: Art. 56(1) provides that the AI Office shall encourage and facilitate the drawing up of codes of practice at Union level in order to contribute to the proper application of this Regulation, taking into account international approaches. Art. 56(2) provides that the AI Office and the AI Board shall aim to ensure that the codes of practice cover at least the obligations provided for in Art. 53 and 55, including: (a) the means whereby to ensure that the information referred to in Art. 53(1)(a) and (b) is kept up to date in light of market and technological developments; (b) the adequate level of detail for the summary about the content used for training; (c) the identification of the type and nature of the systemic risks at Union level, including their sources where appropriate; (d) the measures, procedures, and modalities for the assessment and management of the systemic risks at Union level, including their documentation, which shall be proportionate to the risks, take into account their severity and probability, and take into account the specific challenges of tackling those risks in light of the possible ways in which such risks may emerge and materialise along the AI value chain. Art. 56(3) provides that the AI Office may invite all providers of GPAI models as well as relevant national competent authorities to participate in drawing up codes of practice. Civil society organisations, industry, academia, and other relevant stakeholders such as downstream providers and independent experts may support the process. Art. 56(4) requires the AI Office and AI Board to aim to ensure that codes of practice clearly set out their specific objectives and contain commitments or measures, including KPIs where appropriate, to ensure the achievement of those objectives, and that they duly take into account the needs and interests of all interested parties, including affected persons, at Union level. Art. 56(5) requires the AI Office to aim to ensure that participants in codes of practice report regularly to the AI Office on the implementation of commitments, measures taken, and their outcomes, including as measured against KPIs where appropriate. KPIs and reporting commitments shall take into account the differences in size and capacity between various participants. Art. 56(6) requires the AI Office and AI Board to regularly monitor and evaluate the achievement of the objectives of codes of practice by the participants and their contribution to the proper application of this Regulation. The AI Office and AI Board shall assess whether the codes of practice cover the obligations provided for in Art. 53 and 55, and shall regularly monitor and evaluate the achievement of their objectives. They shall publish their assessment of the adequacy of the codes of practice. The Commission may, by way of implementing act, approve a code of practice and give it a general validity within the Union. That implementing act shall be adopted in accordance with the examination procedure referred to in Art. 98(2). Art. 56(7) provides that the AI Office may invite all providers of GPAI models to adhere to the codes of practice. For providers of GPAI models not posing systemic risks, this adherence may be limited to the obligations laid down in Art. 53, unless they expressly declare their interest to join the full code. Art. 56(8) provides that the AI Office shall also encourage and facilitate the review and adaptation of codes of practice, particularly in the light of emerging standards, and shall assist in the evaluation of available standards. Art. 56(9) provides that codes of practice shall be ready by 2 May 2025. The AI Office shall take the necessary steps, including inviting providers pursuant to paragraph 7. If by 2 August 2025 a code of practice cannot be finalised, or if the AI Office deems it inadequate following its assessment under paragraph 6, the Commission may, by way of implementing acts, lay down common rules for the implementation of the obligations provided for in Art. 53 and 55, including the issues referred to in paragraph 2. Those implementing acts shall be adopted in accordance with the examination procedure referred to in Art. 98(2).
financialSectorGuidance: Relevant for financial institutions using or providing GPAI models. Codes of practice under Art. 56 provide a safe harbour for demonstrating compliance with GPAI obligations (Art. 53/55). Financial institutions integrating GPAI models should monitor whether their GPAI providers have adhered to approved codes of practice, as this directly affects the institution third-party risk assessment. The Commission-approved codes, once published, will serve as a practical benchmark for GPAI due diligence in vendor management under MaRisk AT 9. The 2 May 2025 deadline has passed — institutions should check for published codes.
enforcementConsequence: No direct fine provision for Art. 56 itself — codes of practice provide a compliance pathway; failure to meet underlying Art. 53/55 obligations remains sanctionable

title: National Procedure for AI Systems Posing a Risk
summary: Establishes the national market surveillance procedure for AI systems posing risks to health, safety, or fundamental rights. Market surveillance authorities examine the system, require corrective action within 15 working days, and may impose provisional measures (market withdrawal, recall, prohibition) if the operator fails to act. Notification to the Commission and other Member States is required. Non-conformity causes are categorised: Art. 5 violations, Section 2 non-compliance, standards deficiencies, or Art. 50 non-compliance. Measures are deemed justified after 3 months (30 days for Art. 5 violations) without objection.
body: Art. 79(1) defines AI systems that pose a risk as "products presenting a risk" within the meaning of Art. 3(19) of Regulation (EU) 2019/1020, insofar as they pose risks to health or safety or to the fundamental rights of persons. Art. 79(2) provides that where the market surveillance authority of a Member State has sufficient reason to consider that an AI system poses a risk as referred to in paragraph 1, it shall carry out an evaluation of the AI system concerned in respect of its compliance with all requirements and obligations laid down in this Regulation. Special attention shall be paid to AI systems posing a risk to vulnerable groups. Where risks to fundamental rights are identified, the market surveillance authority shall also inform the relevant national authorities or public bodies referred to in Art. 77(1) and fully cooperate with them. The relevant operators shall cooperate as necessary with the market surveillance authority and the other authorities or public bodies referred to in Art. 77(1). Where, in the course of that evaluation, the market surveillance authority or, where applicable, the market surveillance authority in cooperation with the national authority referred to in Art. 77(1), finds that the AI system does not comply with the requirements and obligations laid down in this Regulation, it shall without delay require the relevant operator to take all appropriate corrective actions to bring the AI system into compliance, to withdraw the AI system from the market, or to recall it within a period the market surveillance authority may prescribe, and in any event within less than 15 working days, or as provided for in the relevant Union harmonisation legislation. Art. 79(3) provides that where the market surveillance authority considers that non-compliance is not restricted to its national territory, it shall inform the Commission and the other Member States without delay of the results of the evaluation and of the actions which it has required the operator to take. Art. 79(4) requires the operator to ensure that all appropriate corrective action is taken in respect of all the AI systems concerned that it has made available on the Union market. Art. 79(5) provides that where the operator of an AI system does not take adequate corrective action within the period referred to in paragraph 2, the market surveillance authority shall take all appropriate provisional measures to prohibit or restrict the AI system being made available on its national market, to withdraw the product or the standalone AI system from that market, or to recall it. That authority shall without delay notify the Commission and the other Member States of those measures. Art. 79(6) requires the notification under paragraph 5 to include all available details, in particular the information necessary for the identification of the non-compliant AI system, the origin of the AI system and the supply chain, the nature of the non-compliance alleged and the risk involved, the nature and duration of the national measures taken, and the arguments put forward by the relevant operator. In particular, the market surveillance authorities shall indicate whether the non-compliance is due to one or more of: (a) non-compliance with the prohibition of AI practices referred to in Art. 5; (b) failure of a high-risk AI system to meet requirements set out in Chapter III Section 2; (c) shortcomings in the harmonised standards or common specifications referred to in Art. 40 and 41 that confer a presumption of conformity; (d) non-compliance with Art. 50. Art. 79(7) requires the market surveillance authorities of other Member States to inform the Commission and the other Member States without delay of any measures adopted and of any additional information at their disposal relating to the non-compliance of the AI system concerned, and, in the event of disagreement with the notified national measure, of their objections. Art. 79(8) provides that where, within three months of receipt of the notification referred to in paragraph 5, no objection has been raised by either a market surveillance authority of a Member State or the Commission against a provisional measure taken by a market surveillance authority of another Member State, that measure shall be deemed justified. The procedural rights of the affected operator under Art. 18 of Regulation (EU) 2019/1020 remain unaffected. The three-month period shall be reduced to 30 days in the case of non-compliance with the prohibition of AI practices referred to in Art. 5. Art. 79(9) requires market surveillance authorities to ensure that appropriate restrictive measures are taken in respect of the product or AI system concerned, such as withdrawal of the product or AI system from their market without delay.
financialSectorGuidance: Directly relevant for financial institutions. Under Art. 74, the financial supervisory authority (BaFin in Germany, FMA in Austria) acts as the market surveillance authority for AI systems used by financial institutions. This means BaFin can invoke Art. 79 to examine any AI system used by a supervised institution, require corrective action within 15 working days, and impose provisional measures (prohibition, withdrawal) if the institution does not comply. Financial institutions should have incident response procedures in place for the scenario where BaFin initiates an Art. 79 evaluation of their credit scoring, insurance pricing, or other AI systems. The 15-working-day corrective action deadline is tight and requires pre-planned remediation capabilities.
enforcementConsequence: No direct fine provision in Art. 79 itself — but the underlying non-compliance triggers fines under Art. 99 (up to EUR 35M/7% for Art. 5 violations, up to EUR 15M/3% for Section 2 non-compliance)

title: Procedure for AI Systems Incorrectly Classified as Non-High-Risk
summary: Establishes the procedure when a market surveillance authority suspects a provider has incorrectly classified an Annex III AI system as non-high-risk under Art. 6(3). The authority examines the classification, requires corrective measures if the system is actually high-risk, notifies the Commission cross-border, and may impose fines under Art. 99 if the provider fails to comply or deliberately misclassified the system to circumvent Chapter III Section 2 requirements. Art. 79(5)-(9) enforcement escalation applies if the provider does not act.
body: Art. 80(1) provides that where a market surveillance authority has sufficient reason to consider that an AI system classified by the provider as non-high-risk pursuant to Art. 6(3) is in fact high-risk, the market surveillance authority shall carry out an evaluation of the AI system concerned in respect of its classification as a high-risk AI system on the basis of the conditions set out in Art. 6(3) and the Commission guidelines. Art. 80(2) provides that where, in the course of that evaluation, the market surveillance authority finds that the AI system concerned is high-risk, it shall without delay require the relevant provider to take all necessary actions to bring the AI system into compliance with the requirements and obligations laid down in this Regulation, as well as to take appropriate corrective action within a period which the market surveillance authority may prescribe. Art. 80(3) provides that where the market surveillance authority considers that the use of the AI system concerned is not restricted to its national territory, it shall inform the Commission and the other Member States without delay of the results of the evaluation and of the actions which it has required the provider to take. Art. 80(4) requires the provider to ensure that all necessary action is taken to bring the AI system into compliance with the requirements and obligations laid down in this Regulation. Where the provider of an affected AI system does not bring the AI system into compliance within the period referred to in paragraph 2, the provider shall be subject to fines in accordance with Art. 99. Art. 80(5) requires the provider to ensure that all appropriate corrective action is taken in respect of all the AI systems concerned that it has made available on the Union market. Art. 80(6) provides that where the provider of the AI system concerned does not take adequate corrective action within the period referred to in paragraph 2, Art. 79(5) to (9) shall apply. Art. 80(7) provides that where, in the course of the evaluation pursuant to paragraph 1, the market surveillance authority establishes that the AI system was misclassified by the provider as non-high-risk in order to circumvent the application of requirements in Chapter III Section 2, the provider shall be subject to fines in accordance with Art. 99. Art. 80(8) provides that in exercising their power to monitor the application of this Article, the market surveillance authorities may carry out appropriate checks in accordance with Art. 11 of Regulation (EU) 2019/1020, taking into account in particular information stored in the EU database referred to in Art. 71 of this Regulation.
financialSectorGuidance: Highly relevant for financial institutions that rely on Art. 6(3) to classify AI systems as non-high-risk despite falling under Annex III categories (e.g. arguing a credit scoring AI does not pose significant risk). BaFin as market surveillance authority can challenge this classification, require full high-risk compliance, and impose Art. 99 fines. Paragraph 7 introduces an aggravated penalty for deliberate misclassification to circumvent Section 2 requirements. Financial institutions should document their Art. 6(3) non-high-risk reasoning thoroughly and defensibly, particularly for AI systems that touch Annex III Nr. 5(b) credit scoring or Nr. 5(c) insurance pricing categories.
enforcementConsequence: No direct fine provision in Art. 80 itself — but non-compliance and deliberate misclassification trigger fines under Art. 99 (up to EUR 15M or 3% of global turnover)
